1) Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra.
The First Chapter of the First Book: The Introduction of the Treatise.
Oṃ, salutation to Vighneśvara [Oṃ, salutation to Gaṇeśa, in manuscripts kh and g]. Mārkaṇḍeya said:
How did the all-pervading Viṣṇu manifest in the form of Hayaśiras in ancient times?
And for what reason did the Lord of Gods assume this beautiful form? || 1 ||
In ancient times, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the master of the universe, [revealed] the Hayashīrṣa;
and you have heard that which was spoken by the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin).
"Tell me, who am asking you, what that first of the Pañcarātras is.
Bhṛgu said:
Listen, my child! I shall proclaim the ancient Pañcarātra.
Having paid homage to the Seven-headed One, since you are a devotee of Keśava,
you ought to hear that ancient Pañcarātra. (4) [The four quarters from "saptī" up to "purātanam" are not present in the manuscripts *kh* and *g*.]

Salutations to the illustrious, illustrious Hayashirsha. 1|2. Regarding the term "Hayashirsha": the connection [of this verse] is with the statement made by Paramesthin (Brahma), following the previous verse which was heard [by him]: "For what purpose did the Lord Narayana, the Master of the World, assume a horse-headed body? Thus it is linked.
4 | He states the utility of listening to the present treatise with the words beginning "saptiśīrṣam" (p. 2): "saptiśīrṣam" means having the head of a horse.
In ancient times, it is said, Maheśvara, together with Gaurī,
questioned the Four-faced One (Brahmā) as he was seated in the palace of Vairāja.
Maheśvara said:
"In former times, you questioned the all-pervading Hayaśiras regarding the Pañcarātra;
he is the Lord who slew Madhu and Kaiṭabha while the universe was submerged in the waters of the single ocean."

O Four-faced One, O Mahāmati, explain all that to me in detail—concerning the four Vedas as they were offered up to the gods. (Note: In the manuscripts designated kh, g, and k, the reading is *manaṃ*.)
Brahmā said:
When the world had become a single ocean difficult to behold, when all moving and stationary beings had perished, and when the moon, sun, and wind had vanished along with the planets and stars; (8)
5. In the reading *sthitam*, it is an adjective qualifying Caturmukha; in the reading *sthitaḥ*, it is an adjective qualifying Maheśvara, meaning "having arrived there and remained. 6.
*Saikārṇavajale*—this is an adjective for the implied term *bhūtale* (on the surface of the earth).

7. Regarding the phrase "when they were restored": the meaning is that when the Vedas had been restored—after Madhu and Kaiṭabha, who had entered Rasātala having stolen the Vedas from you, had been slain and those [Vedas] had been recovered and returned to you by the Lord in his Hayagrīva form.
8. Here, after the words "Brahmā said," [the following occurs]:

The reading "He quickly divided the golden orb into two" (*dvidhā cakāra vai tūrṇaṃ maṇḍalaṃ tu hiraṇmayam*) is seen as an interpolation in the *Kha* and *Ga* manuscripts; however, since the golden egg (*hiraṇyāṇḍa*) is out of place here in the context of describing the dissolution of the primary elements (*prakṛtapralaya*), [the correct reading should be:
"Then the Lord Nārāyaṇa created by means of that splendor," as will be stated later in the passage beginning with "the Blessed One [created] the golden egg" (*hiraṇyamaṇḍaṃ bhagavān*).

For, having begun with the words "Then the Blessed Self-existent One," it is stated in the fourteenth verse and further by the statement of Manu, "That egg became golden," that the production of the golden egg is described as occurring at the very moment preceding creation; thus [it says]: "I quickly divided the golden sphere into two."
Having assumed the remaining paryaṅka posture according to the text to be explained later (p. 3), while the god Janārdana is asleep;
Listen indeed to what occurred long ago when the world was a single ocean of water.
He who lies in the midst of the ocean, resting upon the serpent-couch,
is the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Blessed One, the primordial God, the ancient one.
Having indeed withdrawn all the worlds and come under the sway of yogic sleep,
there was a great divine splendor within the body of that sleeping Lord.
From the navel, in the form of a lotus, there emerged a great abundance;
that lotus blazed like a lamp through the splendor of Viṣṇu. || 12 ||
Then the god Nārāyaṇa, resembling a thousand suns, indeed created [the lotus] with its thousand petals and filaments by means of that splendor.
The Blessed One was the golden egg; within it, I again quickly divided that golden egg into two parts. || 14 ||
And there, this great form appeared: "This golden form of mine has four arms, four faces, and is adorned with a crown of matted locks. (15)

This portion has not been included in the root text because it would result in the fault of excessive reduplication (pīnaruktya) and because it was not accepted in the most ancient manuscript known as the *saṃjñita*. Furthermore,
the absence of the augment *aṭ* in the form "sṛjat" is an archaic (ārṣa) usage.

14. Regarding the word *garbha*: the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is "In that egg, having become the embryo (*garbha*), I divided that egg into two. This is in agreement with the statement of Manu: "Having dwelt in that egg for a full year, that Blessed Lord, by his own meditation, made that egg twofold. Even if the reading is *cakāra* ("he made"), it refers to "I" (*aham*).
Thus it should be applied: "Being of such a form, I am established upon that lotus."
At that time, you mastered the Vedas, along with their limbs (aṅgas), secondary limbs (upāṅgas), and the methods of Pada and Krama recitation. || 16 ||
Then the Vedas waited upon me as I was embodied;
while I was intent on the study of the Vedas there, a drop of sweat was produced.
Having reached a lotus leaf, it then split into two and fell;
from that were born two Daityas, fierce in their strength and composed of rajas and tamas.
Then those two named Madhu and Kaiṭabha, possessed of great strength and prowess and fixed in their sinful resolve, indeed stole my Vedas.
Then, when the Vedas along with their bodies had been stolen,
that god Maheśvara was awakened by me from the mouth of Padmanābha.
15. "With four arms"—this is indeed a traditional teaching from the Ṛṣis.
19. "Of evil resolve"—this is a significant qualification; it means [they act] with the intent to destroy the Vedas that establish sacrifices and the like, and not out of respect for them.

20. "In those with bodies" (*saśarīreṣu*) means in those accompanied by their limbs (*sāṅgeṣu*), that is to say, together with the auxiliary sciences such as *Śikṣā* and *Kalpa*. In the reading without the visarga (*nirvisargapāṭhe*), "Maheśvara" is an address to Śiva. In the reading with the visarga (*savisargapāṭhe*), however, it is an attribute of the word "Devā"; in that case, the word *maheśvara* does not denote Śiva.

Regarding the phrase "of Padmanābha": from the mouth of Padmanābha, this Lord, the Blessed Viṣṇu, was awakened by me—that is, made manifest through hymns of praise and other means. By the statement "thereupon that God, having become fully awake, assumed the form of Hayagrīva," [it is shown that] the second [form], consisting of Hayagrīva, manifested from the mouth of Bālamukunda who was lying within the Garbhodaka ocean.

It must be understood that this refers to His form; otherwise, the passage to be cited later—"having gone to the depths of the Rasātala with his second body"—would be untenable. Now, if by the phrase "with his second body" it were meant that the Lord [remained] in the Garbhodaka-śaya itself in His own form...
Then that Lord, having awakened, assumed the form of Hayagrīva,
resembling a hundred moons and adorned with various ornaments. (21)
Four-armed, bearing a mace, a discus, a lotus, and a bow, and auspicious;
with his second body, he went to the depths of the netherworld. || 22 ||
Having gone with that horse-headed form and taken the eternal Vedas,
he went to the divine abode of Pūṣan,
which is frequented by hosts of great sages.
That teacher of the world likewise bestowed the Vedas once again;
listen to me as I relate what was asked of the Lord by me at that time.
How many *pañcarātra* scriptures were indeed spoken by you in the past?
O Lord, how is your installation performed by those desiring liberation—or, as noted in the marginal gloss, enjoyment or devotion? (25)

It is stated that [the Lord] abandoned His second form consisting of Hayashirsha and assumed [another]; however, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the word *padmanābhasya*, which indicates a sense of difference, and the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in the word *ānanāt*, which indicates the source of departure, are both untenable. Therefore, in that assembly, the Blessed Lord Hayashirshatha was present in person as the Sacrificial Person (*yajñapuruṣa*), possessing the color of refined gold.

Thus, by the eleventh verse of the seventeenth chapter of the second book of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, which begins with "consisting of Vedic meters" (*chandomaya*) and "consisting of sacrifices" (*makhamaya*), and likewise by the [verse] from the eleventh book: "Viṣṇu descended as a partial incarnation for the sake of Śiva; by him, the Madhubhit, the Vedas were recovered from Hayagrīva."

Since it is established by the seventeenth verse of the fourth chapter that [this being] is indeed another [form], appearing as a partial incarnation (*aṃśāvatāra*), it is thus justified that this horse-headed one named Hayaśīrṣa is distinct from Garbhodaśāyī and others; therefore, everything is clear.
Here, regarding the passage beginning with "born from the ear-wax of Viṣṇu," etc., from the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*—
The contradiction with the statements in the *Devīmāhātmya*, however, is to be resolved by means of the distinction between different *kalpas*. (p.
6) And what, O Lord, are the characteristics of the teachers (*ācāryas*) and the image-keepers (*mūrtipās*)? [The passage beginning with "O Teacher," etc., O Lord...]
The two verses ending with "ityantaṃ" are not present in the manuscripts Kh and G;
[they concern] the procedure for the Vāstuyāga and likewise the rule for the offering of the *arghya*.
The procedure for the installation of the stone, as well as the means of accomplishing the sacred site and so forth;
the characteristics of the temple, and likewise the characteristics of the image. || 27 ||

O Lord of the Gods, all five types of consecrations, as well as the procedure for hoisting the banner, and whatever else may be required as a subsidiary part of the consecration that has been asked about—[all this I shall explain]. 28.
O Lord! Whatever I have failed to recite, whether through ignorance or through negligence, you should kindly explain all of that in its entirety out of your grace. (29)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Introduction of the Scripture," in the Ādikāṇḍa of the *Hayaśīrṣa-mahāpañcarātra*, the twelve-thousand-verse [work].
[In manuscripts kh and g, this is the first chapter; in manuscript k, it is the first section. || 1 ||
The cumulative count of verses from the beginning is 29.
The words ending in the accusative case, such as *arghyadānavidhim* and so forth, are to be construed with the phrase *vaktum arhasi*.
(Verse 29) Regarding the phrase *tatsarvam akhilam*: *sarvam* is the object (*karman*), while *akhilam* is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).
The meaning is "by means of the totality"; therefore, there is no tautology.
Second Chapter.
(An Exposition of the Nature of Pañcarātra) The Blessed Lord said:
"I shall tell you all that which was asked by you in its entirety."
The five nights were proclaimed by me in former times, in kalpa after kalpa. || 1 ||
These have been categorized by the sages in the world as twenty-five in number;
the Hayashirsha is proclaimed as the first among all the tantras.
The Trailokyamohana Tantra, the Vaibhava, and likewise the Pauṣkara; the Nāradīya Tantra, as well as the Prāhrāda, the Gārgya, and the Gālava.
The Śrīpraśna, the Śāṇḍilya-tantra, the Īśvarasaṃhitā-tantra,
the excellent Satyokta-tantra,
as well as the Vāsiṣṭha and the Śaunaka. || 4 ||
Furthermore, there is the Nārāyaṇīya Tantra, as well as the Jñānārṇava;
also the Svāyambhuva, the Kāpila, and likewise the Vihagendra. (5)
The Ātreya, the one called Nārasiṃha, the one called Ānanda, as well as the Āruṇa;
likewise the Baudhāyana Tantra, and the Tantra proclaimed by Viśvāmitra.

1. By the phrase "thus proclaimed," the proponents of their [the Pāñcarātras'] having a beginning (*sāditva*) are refuted, since it is stated that the *Pañcarātras* are beginningless (*anādi*) by virtue of being a continuous stream (*pravāha*).
2. "The first" (*ādyam*) means that which exists at the beginning; for it was spoken by the Lord at the very outset, prior to creation.
The procedure of the eight syllables is called the Great Tantra;
these [teachings], both in brief and in detail, remain pervading the surface of the earth. (7)
The Tantra of the Bhāgavatas spoken by Śiva and uttered by Viṣṇu,
as well as the Padmodbhava Purāṇa and another, the Vārāha.
These are the common compendiums of the Bhāgavatas;
there is another compendium spoken by Vyāsa, as well as the Paramasaṃhitā.
Whatever else has been sung by the sages is indeed based upon these very [teachings];
and all that pertains to the installation and other such matters was spoken by Viṣṇu.
Whoever desires to perform the merit of the consecration of my image must seek out a preceptor endowed with the auspicious marks. || 11 ||
But that wise one born of the Kula who, being purified in the womb of Brahman, knows the dissolution, origination, and maintenance [of the universe], he is worthy of the office of an Ācārya.
A Brāhmaṇa who is an expert in the Pañcarātra among all the social orders, who is completely free from anger and greed, and devoid of fault and envy; || 13 ||

10. Regarding the phrase "whatever else": by this it should be understood that, while the twenty-five [treatises] previously mentioned are primarily designated by the term *Pañcarātra*, other works devoted to the worship of the Lord—such as the *Tantras*, *Purāṇas*, and so forth—are included within the *Pañcarātra* scriptures themselves. Consequently, whatever is devoted to the worship of the Lord...
It appears that this very scripture is indeed the *Pañcarātra*.

Regarding the phrase "to perform"— having defined the nature of the *Pañcarātra*, he states the characteristics of the preceptor suitable for the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) by means of the passage beginning with "desiring to perform," and so forth.
Free from consumption and epilepsy, devoid of the disease of leprosy,
with limbs neither deficient nor redundant, he is a youth endowed with auspicious marks. (14)
Devoted to no other deity and avoiding the food of Śūdras,
in the absence of Brāhmaṇas, a Kṣatriya is prescribed for Vaiśyas and Śūdras;
and in the absence of Kṣatriyas, a Vaiśya is prescribed for a Śūdra.
A Śūdra, however, is never at any time worthy of the status of a teacher. || 16 ||
One should always make a householder or one established in celibacy his guru— one who is free from the eight faults beginning with 'ka' and is devoted to the vow of fasting.

13. Regarding the term "Brāhmaṇa": this states that, as appropriate, the status of being a teacher belongs to those of the three higher castes, while it is unattainable for Śūdras. Among them, a Brāhmaṇa [is the teacher] for the four castes beginning with himself; in the absence of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya [is the teacher] for Vaiśyas and Śūdras; and in the absence of a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya [is the teacher].

With the words beginning with "brāhmaṇa" and ending with "arhati," he begins to state that while a Brāhmaṇa possesses the qualification for being a teacher (*ācārya*) of a Śūdra, a Śūdra has no qualification for that role whatsoever. The meaning is that a Brāhmaṇa endowed with the qualities to be described hereafter and proficient in the Pañcarātra is the teacher of all social classes (*varṇas*).

15. Regarding the term *ananya* (non-dual/devoted to none other): it refers to one who is devoted to no other deity, being intent on the worship of the deity to be installed. This is because, as stated in the *Tantrasāra*:

"In the Vaiṣṇava [tradition], a Vaiṣṇava is to be accepted; in the Śaiva, a Śaiva; and in the Śākta, [a Śākta]," and so forth—thus praising only those who are worshippers of their respective deities as being fit for the office of *ācārya* in those respective contexts. It does not, however, refer to one who hates other deities.

Because of the prohibition regarding [the status of] a guru in the statement from the third chapter beginning with "one who reviles the twice-born, the guru, and the gods" (verse 17). Regarding the phrase "a householder," etc.—this means a householder who is established in celibacy (*brahmacarya*). For the celibacy of a householder is prohibited by such statements of Manu as: "Of those [wives], however, the first four are [permissible], but the eleventh is likewise censured. Etc.

It should be understood that one should approach one's wife during her fertile period (*ṛtu*), preceded by the avoidance of specific nights; this refers to the practice of approaching her during the fertile period as established by such scriptural injunctions as "one should be a visitor during the fertile period. One should avoid women on the eight censured nights and on the other [prohibited] nights; for by doing so, one remains a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) regardless of which stage of life (*āśrama*) one inhabits. Thus it is said.

This is because it accords with the words of Manu. Nor should it be argued that this statement—"the householder and the one established in celibacy"—is intended to express a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), for [he] is a knower of the meaning of all the scriptures.
When the Supreme Person was established by such a teacher— one who is upright in nature and speaks with a sweet smile— (18)
The ruler of that region, the sacrificer, the artisans, the architects, and so forth—all of them will rejoice for a very long time; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, in the *Hayaśīrṣa Mahāpañcarātra*, in the twelve-thousand-verse work, in the first section.
The second chapter, titled "An Exposition on the Essential Nature of the Pañcarātra. || 2 ||

The total number of verses from the beginning is 48. A householder may be the officiating preceptor (*deśika*) for rites dedicated to the gods (*daiva*), the ancestors (*pitrya*), and mixed rites (*miśra*). This is established by the two scriptural citations from the *Kulārṇava* and the *Yāmala*, as cited in the *Āgamatattvavilāsa*: "A householder may be the officiating preceptor in rites for the gods, the ancestors, and mixed rites."

It should be understood that this is because the qualification for the office of preceptor is heard to belong only to householders, and because the forthcoming statement in the third chapter— namely, "the Śaiva, the Saura, the Naiṣṭhika," and so forth— demonstrates by its own words that those who have taken lifelong vows (naiṣṭhikas) lack qualification in this matter.
18. Regarding the word *bhāṣiṇam*, the suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of habitual disposition (*tācchīlye*), meaning one whose nature is to speak preceded by a smile.
However, if the reading were *bhāṣitam*, that meaning would not be applicable. (p.
The Third Chapter (The Characteristics of the Teacher to be Avoided).
The Blessed One said:
I shall now describe those installers who possess contrary qualities; one should not have the consecration performed by those who are excluded from this tantra. (1)

A Śaiva, a Saura, one who has taken lifelong vows, a naked ascetic, one born of a mixed caste, an impure person, an elderly man, one of loathsome appearance, or one marked by a great sin (mahāpātaka). || 2 ||

One who suffers from leprosy, one with deformed nails, one with white leucoderma, one with black teeth, as well as one suffering from consumption; one born in the region of Kaccha, or from the lands of Kāverī, Koṅkaṇa, and Oṅga; || 3 ||
He is born in Kāmarūpa, Kaliṅga, Kāñcī, Kāśmīra, and Kośala;
he is of evil conduct and of evil association, and he originates from Mahārāṣṭra. || 4 ||
Then there was Kubuddhi (Evil-minded), Kuvṛtti (Evil-conduct), Lamboṣṭhī (Long-lipped), Niṣṭhīvī (Spitter),
Ghargharasvara (Gurgling-voiced),
Arbudī (Goitered), Gāruḍī (Garuda-like), Vyaṅga (Deformed), Garvita (Arrogant), and likewise Badhira (Deaf). || 5 ||

1 | He states the characteristics of the teacher to be avoided—beginning with "sthāpakān. *Sthāpaka*, *guru*, *ācārya*, *deśika*, and so forth, are synonymous terms. Regarding "by means of contrary qualities" (*viparītaguṇaiḥ*): this means by means of censurable qualities that are the opposite of the praiseworthy qualities previously mentioned, such as being of pure Brahmanic origin and knowing the dissolution, creation, and maintenance [of the universe].

2 | From the words "The Śaiva [teacher] says" up to the end of the chapter, he states those things to be avoided. 5 | Here, the reading "kuvṛttiḥ" found in the manuscripts Kh and G has not been included in the root text, because it would result in redundancy with what was stated in the preceding verse. The reading "niṣṭhīvadhardharasvaraḥ" found in the manuscripts Kh and G...
The reading [on page 12] is not accepted:
"One who hates the Tantras and likewise one who delights in harming others."
One who is deformed, has a voice like a crow, is impotent, cowardly, and likewise prone to anger.

One who has remarried, one born of oneself, one with testicles like a ball, an atheist, as well as one who is dull-witted, excessively pale, bald, or lacking a limb, or indeed one who is corpulent. || 7 ||
One who is excessively dark-complexioned, merciless, sinful, emaciated, short, lazy, as well as diseased, uncultivated, anxious, or indeed miserable; || 8 ||
One who is devoid of vows and fasts, a husband of a *vṛṣalī*, one who subsists by means of trade and stage-plays, and one who is a trafficker in women or an adulterer; || 9 ||

*Niṣṭhīvaḥ* means the act of spitting out phlegm from the mouth; because of that, there is an absence of a gurgling voice (*ghargharasvara*). However, according to the accepted reading, *niṣṭhīvī* refers to one who constantly spits phlegm from the mouth;
such a person has a gurgling voice caused by the provocation of phlegm and so forth—a harsh voice like that of a camel—and this meaning would be more appropriate.

6. One who hates the Tantras and hates the Śāstras, because he is incapable of devotion toward the Blessed One, who is the subject taught by those Śāstras, and toward [rituals] such as consecration (pratiṣṭhā). A *kuṇḍa* is one born from another man’s wife while her husband is still living.
7. Regarding the term *golaka*: a *golaka* is one born from another man’s wife whose husband is deceased. A *khalvāṭa* is one suffering from *indraluptika* (baldness).

The meaning is that his hair has fallen out due to its inherent nature. As Bhartṛhari says in the *Nītiśataka*: "A bald man, his head scorched by the rays of the sun, went seeking a place free from the heat; moving with quick steps, he came to the foot of a palm tree."
One who hates the sons of the teacher and others, one who serves others, one who eats [forbidden food], a servant, one who is addicted to vices, a slanderer, and one who speaks harshly; (10) p. 13)

One who is chronically ill, a physician, one who acts with rashness, one who has fallen away from his vows, a reviler of the twice-born, of gurus, and of the gods, as well as an installer [of images], || 11 ||
One with tawny eyes, one with honey-colored eyes, one with smoke-colored eyes, and likewise one with cat-like eyes;
one who is envious, one with scrofulous swellings on the neck, and one who follows the conduct of a crow. || 12 ||
Lacking instruction in skillful means, he is harsh, cruel, and follows contemptible vows;
he is merciless, devoid of compassion, and bereft of proficiency. || 13 ||
One who knows the methods of the *pratiṣṭhā* tantras and has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅgas*)—
even if he is all-knowing— one should diligently avoid an atheist (*nāstika*). (14)
10. Regarding "ācārya": one who harbors hatred toward the teacher (*ācārya*), the spiritual sons (*putraka*), and so forth, yet serves others.

The meaning is: one who manifests hostility toward the teacher, the spiritual sons, and their like, while simultaneously practicing compliance—like a servant—toward others, whoever they may be. According to Amara: "A *sevaka* is a dependent (*anujīvī*); those who serve are dependents."

Therefore, there is no tautology with the second word *sevaka*. Regarding the term *piśuna*: since the word *piśuna* functions as an adjective, the suffix *-in* could not be applied to it; thus, the reading *piśunī* was not included in the root text.
13. Regarding *kakkhaṭa*: it means one whose nature is harsh (*niṣṭhuraprakṛti*). *Kakkhaṭa*, *kaṭhina*, *krūra*, and *kaṭhora* [are synonyms].
"Niṣṭhura" means "firm," according to Amara [Kośa] (14).

Regarding "pratiṣṭhā"—the meaning is that even if one is an expert in the principles of the *Pratiṣṭhā-tantra*, if he has not mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*), then he is to be avoided. This refers to one who, failing to attain proficiency in the Vedas, the auxiliary sciences, and so forth, [yet claims to be] an expounder of the *Pratiṣṭhā*.
One who knows the words, sentences, and means of valid cognition according to the scriptures— a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.
One who is colored by the scriptures of the bound (paśu) is neither a teacher nor a guide. || 15 ||
The God, established by these, bestows fruit; he can never be rendered impure.

If the installation of Viṣṇu is performed anywhere while devoid of these [qualities], it will not be effective for either worldly enjoyment or liberation; it is fruitless, of this there is no doubt. || 17 ||
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Teachers to be Avoided," in the Ādikāṇḍa of the *Hayaśīrṣa Mahāpañcarātra*, the twelve-thousand-verse [work]. || 3 ||
The cumulative number of verses from the beginning is 65.

It should be noted that for one who knows only the mere sequence [of words], there can be no specific knowledge regarding sacrifices and the like involving their respective procedures (*itikartavyatā*); therefore, such a person must be excluded. However, according to the reading of manuscripts *kha* and *ga*:

The meaning is that even one who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, if he knows only a little regarding the *Pratiṣṭhātantras* or possesses immature knowledge concerning the *Pratiṣṭhātantras*, is to be avoided. (15) Even one who knows the words, sentences, and means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and even one who has mastered the Vedas, [is to be avoided] by means of the *paśuśāstra*.
The meaning is that if one's intellect is colored by a treatise that contradicts the knowledge derived from the Vedic teachings, he does not possess the status of a teacher.
(p. 15) The Fourth Chapter.
(The Characteristics of the Teacher) The Blessed One said: Furthermore, I shall specifically explain the characteristics of the teacher. || 1 ||
Space, wind, fire, water, and likewise earth—
these indeed are known as nights; they are insentient and characterized by the predominance of tamas.
Furthermore, when one realizes that reality which is distinct from these very nights and is stainless,
then one is proclaimed as liberated.
Then that Blessed One, Viṣṇu, is undoubtedly the Supreme Self. || 4 ||

1. In the second chapter, by means of the passage beginning with "the teacher who is the perfectly pure womb of Brahman," the teacher has been characterized in general; here, he characterizes him specifically by means of the passage beginning with "viśeṣeṇa" (by distinction).
2. Regarding the word "ākāśa": it means the five categories of elements, beginning with space and ending with earth.

The nights are well-known. He states the reason for this: "For they are insentient" (hyacaitanyeti). For (hi) because space and the other elements are insentient—that is, devoid of consciousness and inert (jaḍa)—and they are dominated by darkness (tamotkaṭāḥ), meaning they possess the quality of *tamas* in excess, since they are produced from the portion of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) in which *tamas* predominates, following the sequence of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
Therefore, the meaning is that their status as "nights" must be accepted due to their common characteristics, such as insentience (*jaḍatva*) and the quality of obscuring (*āvarakatva*).

(3-4) He states the fruit of this demonstration with the words "of the nights": one whose means [of purification] have been perfected, whose mind has become stainless through the power of austerity (*tapas*), whose intellect is washed by the waters of discrimination (*viveka*), and whose bonds of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) have been utterly severed.
When one realizes that reality— the Supreme Self— which is distinct from and separate from these aforementioned nights denoted by the word "night," being stainless and free from limiting adjuncts;
[realizing] that this Supreme Self, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and is different from the insentient world.
Even if he is of evil conduct and devoid of all auspicious marks,
he should be known as a teacher who ferries one across the ocean of saṃsāra. (5)
That twice-born man who perceives the Self as distinct in all things, even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks, is a guru; of this there is no doubt.
O best of the twice-born, that foremost of brahmins who knows this Saṃhitā in its four quarters is entitled to perform a sacrifice, even if he is devoid of all other auspicious marks.
But one who has awakened through the Pañcarātra and knows the reality of this Siddhānta is distinguished as an Ācārya, even if he is devoid of all [other] characteristics. || 8 ||

The meaning is that when one thus ascertains the reality of things (*vastutatva*), then one is proclaimed "liberated. At that moment—namely, at the instant of such knowledge—one who has ascertained the reality of things is "liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*); the meaning is that he becomes like the Supreme Self, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu. This is according to the Vedic scripture: "The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself."
5. He describes the teacherhood of such a knower of the Supreme Self with the words beginning with "even" (*api*).

Even one whose conduct is sinful—meaning one who, due to indifference toward daily and occasional obligatory rites such as the *saṃdhyā-vandana*, and due to indifference toward the conduct prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, is regarded by worldly perception as being a sinner—even such a person [is a teacher].
Even if he lacks all the [traditional] characteristics— meaning even if he is devoid of the previously mentioned characteristics of a teacher such as being born from the pure source of Brahman—

he alone is to be known as the true Guru, the one who ferries [disciples] across the ocean of saṃsāra. The meaning is that when the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) is performed by such a teacher, liberation is inevitable.
6. He demonstrates this very same point in brief for the sake of worldly understanding with the words "everywhere.

7. He states another method of the Teacher: "consisting of four quarters. That best of the twice-born who [studies] this Saṃhitā consisting of four quarters, namely the four quarters beginning with Ādi and Saṅkarṣaṇa...

The meaning is that he who knows the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*— which establishes the forms of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), its ancillaries, temples, images, and their various implements— is fit for the office of an *ācārya*, independent of all other [secular] characteristics.

8 | He states another type of teacher: "In the *Pañcarātra*," etc. In the *Pañcarātra* scripture, wherever it may be, one who is not a *tāraka* (savior) is never [to be accepted]; by such a person, no sacrifice (*yajña*) should be performed.
O sinless one, when a guru is devoid of knowledge yet has correctly awakened to the reality of the ultimate truth, he is considered a "liberator" (tāraka). || 9 ||
He whose supreme devotion to Viṣṇu is equal to his devotion to the Guru—he alone is to be known as the true establisher; this I tell you as the truth. 10.
But he who, deluded by greed for consecration, should perform an initiation, goes to a terrible hell along with his disciples; of this there is no doubt. (11)
Thus ends the fourth chapter, on the characteristics of the preceptor, in the Ādikāṇḍa of the *Hayaśīrṣa Mahāpañcarātra*, the twelve-thousand-verse [treatise]. || 4 ||

The total number of verses from the beginning is 76; for otherwise, there would be the fault of redundancy with what was previously stated in the *Hayaśīrṣa*. "Awakened" (*prabuddha*) means endowed with supreme knowledge;
likewise, he is a knower of the reality of the established doctrine (*siddhāntārtha*), which consists of the worship of the Lord as propounded in the *Pañcarātra*.

The meaning is that an Ācārya who possesses the knowledge of reality regarding that [subject] is distinguished even if he lacks all other characteristics. Since the *Pañcarātra* scripture is devoted to the worship of the Lord, when there is excellence in that knowledge, one is distinguished from those outside the *Pañcarātra*— even if they are characterized by various other marks— without depending on any other characteristics.
The distinction residing in the teacher is to be noted.
(10) Regarding the phrase "of whom": the meaning is that the very knowledge of the non-difference between the guru and the deity is the essential nature of devotion.
The Fifth Chapter: (The determination of those ineligible for this scripture, the fixed directions for consecration, and the examination of the ground.)
The Blessed One said:
This should not be spoken to those who argue from mere logic, nor in the presence of atheists.
Jaimini, the Sugata, the Nihilist, the Naked One (the Jaina), Kapila, and Akṣapāda—these six are the proponents of logical reasoning. || 2 ||
Those lowest of men who act in accordance with this view are called proponents of causalism (*hetuvādins*); one should not bestow the *tantra* upon them. (3)
Now, listen to me as I describe how the gods should be installed in a city according to the auspicious rules for the placement of deities, including the regulations regarding the cardinal directions.

1. Now, he defines those who are not qualified for this scripture with the words beginning "this" (*idam*). The meaning is that this scripture must not be taught to the proponents of *hetuvāda* (rationalism) to be mentioned later, nor to the foremost of the nihilists (*nāstika*). *Āstikya* is the conviction that there exists a reality accessible solely through the Vedas. (Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā 3.28)

Thus, because those logicians— who fall outside the definition of faith (*āstikyā*), who especially rely upon reasoning, and who, by relying on counter-arguments, seek to establish the invalidity of those scriptures devoted to the worship of the Blessed One— are included within the category of atheists (*nāstika*), whoever would despise them...

And because [such people] are censured by such statements as: "A twice-born man who at its root relies upon the science of logic (*hetu-śāstra*)—that atheist (*nāstika*) who reviles the Vedas—should be expelled by the virtuous" (Manu 2.22). Here, although atheists are already included by virtue of being proponents of logic (*hetuvādin*), the specific mention of "at the head of atheists" (*nāstikāgrataḥ*) is for the purpose of their particular exclusion. [This applies] in the reading *nāstikā yataḥ*.
This should not be spoken to those who propound causality (*hetuvādins*), because the meaning is that those proponents of causality are nihilists (*nāstikas*).
(2) He defines the aforementioned proponents of causality with the words beginning "Jaimini" and so forth.
(3) He states the fault in following their doctrine with the words beginning "this" (*etad*) and so forth.

4. Regarding the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), he states the rule for the distinction of directions according to the specific deity, beginning with "Now" (*atha*) and ending with "is divided" (*bhidyate*). (p.
19) "In the center of a city or village, however, the place of Brahmā is supreme."
To the east is the auspicious abode of Ākhaṇḍala, the Sun. || 5 ||
To the south of the Mothers, situated in its own direction from Agni,
is the abode of the Bhūtas, where the auspicious residence of Dharmarāja is located.
The region of Caṇḍikā, the Pitṛs, and the Daityas shall be in the southwest;
that of Pracetas, the Ocean, and the Rivers shall be in the west.
And for the hooded serpents, the auspicious abode of Vāyu is in the northwest;
and for Skanda, the lord of the Yakṣas, his abode is said to be in the north.
The station of Caṇḍīśa Maheśa is desired in the northeast;
however, the station of Viṣṇu is everywhere, though it varies according to the difference in time.
All of them were established facing the city, bestowing auspiciousness upon men. || 10 ||
If they have turned their faces away [from the practice] due to ignorance or negligence, then the wise man should employ this following means according to the scriptures and other authorities. (11)
Endowed with that same color and ornaments, and possessing those same weapons and vehicles,
one should depict that deity there upon the wall facing the city.

10. Thus, although there is a fixed rule regarding the directions based on the specific deities in the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), he states that "facing the city" must be observed everywhere with the words "facing the city.
11. He provides a remedy for the eventuality of being turned away from that [direction] by fate, using two verses beginning with "through ignorance."
Having first leveled the temple site, one who is wise should not construct a small palace there that is either equal to or larger than the original [structure]. (13)
Having left a boundary twice the height of the structure on both sides,
a wise man should have another palace built so that neither side is oppressed.
O best of gods, listen with focused attention to my location according to the specific directions:
whether in the middle of a village or in the forest (or in a wilderness).
Likewise on a mountain, in a forest, or at the confluence of rivers. || 15 ||
I am established everywhere all around the city, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men; listen now to another special distinction. (16)
In the eastern direction it is praised for prosperity; in the southeastern direction it is praised [and should be known as highly commended], but one should avoid it [having avoided it].
In the southern direction it is praised for peace; in the southwestern direction it will bring fear. || 17 ||

13 | Regarding the word "pūrva" (previously): the meaning is that one must not, after demolishing a previously built temple that is undesirable, construct another temple there according to one's own preference— whether it be smaller, equal, or larger in dimension than the original.

14. Then, when a powerful desire arises to construct a new palace on that very site, he says "of both" regarding what should be done: having left a boundary equal to the height of both sides of the previously situated palace—that is, a measurement double the dimension of the height of that palace.
One should construct another palace, but not in the middle of that one; thus he says, "not both.
(15) Therein, according to the distinction of desires, he states the specific directions with the verse beginning with "direction" and ending with "of the three.
For the sake of attaining wealth and other goals, one should diligently avoid [the northeast]; for the attainment of sovereignty, one should avoid [the east];
for the increase of prosperity, one should avoid [the north]. (18)
Sacrifice performed in the northeast is most excellent, bestowing all prosperity upon men;
having understood this, one should specifically examine the ground thereafter. (19)
The characteristics of that best of teachers are now described:
it is there that female deer take delight together with their calves and the bulls. (20)
O best of men, it was there that beautiful women enjoyed pleasure with men;
formerly, it was the residence of kings, as well as of sacrificial priests and their sacred fires.

Fragrant with the scent of Kāśmīra sandalwood, possessing the aroma of camphor and agallochum, and bearing the fragrance of lotuses and water-lilies, as well as the scent of jasmine and campaka flowers. || 22 ||
She has the fragrance of the pāṭalā and mallikā flowers; she possesses the scent of nāgakeśara;
she has the aroma of curd, milk, and clarified butter; and she bears the fragrance of wine and spirits.
The earth, which possesses the fragrance of fragrant rice and the sound of auspicious objects,
is considered the common ground for all social classes.

20. Now, the examination of the ground suitable for the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) is described. Regarding that, first he states the characteristics of an auspicious site with the verse beginning "of fragrant [plants]," etc.
Foul-smelling, painful, and of various colors, it is difficult to endure;
shaped like a circle or a half-moon, it is twice as long as it is wide. (25)
Vikarṇā, Karṇahīnā, Vakrā, Sūcīmukhī, Dvikarṇā, Sūrpa-sadṛśī, Gomukhī, and Trikoṇikā. || 26 ||
That which is hexagonal, resembling a trident, or like the back of an elephant;
that which is like a reptile, confused in direction, or shaped like a cart. (27)
A ground of such a kind should be avoided with great effort by the instructors.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, "The Characteristics of the Earth," in the Ādikāṇḍa of the *Hayaśīrṣa Mahāpañcarātra*, the twelve-thousand-verse [treatise].
The total number of verses from the beginning is 204.25.

Regarding that, he describes the characteristics of the censured ground from the verse beginning with *durgandha* up to the end of the chapter. Here, in the phrase *duḥpura*, the reading *durbhaga* is seen in the *Śabdakalpadruma* under the entry for the word *mandira*, within the description of the ground according to the *Hayaśīrṣa*.
Sixth Chapter:
(Examination and Purification of the Ground)
The Blessed One said:
The ground for a temple is specifically declared to be of four kinds.
Supadmā, Bhadrikā, Pūrṇā, Dhūmrāvegī, and another [named Aparā]. || 1 ||

It was adorned with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, with the *arjuna* trees of auspicious sound; it was beautified by *punnāga*, *pārśva*, and *candana* trees, as well as *sarala*, *arjuna*, *tilaka*, coconut palms, and *kāśa* grass.
Abounding with lotuses and water-lilies, it is renowned as Supadmā;
it is beautified by rivers, oceans, sacred sites, and mountain ranges.
It was strewn with flowering trees and adorned with milky trees;
it was completely covered by forest groves, gardens, creepers, shrubs, and blossoming thickets.

1. Having described in the previous chapter the general characteristics of lands that are prescribed or prohibited, [the author] here states their specific varieties along with their defining marks, beginning with the words "supadma" and so forth. The term "āveginī" is a qualifier for "dhūmrā. The other [type of land], which is distinct from the three previously mentioned auspicious lands, is the "āveginī."
The earth is called "smoky" (dhūmrā) because it is agitated by gravel, thorns, vultures, and the like. In this context, the reading found in the *Vaidikasarvasva* is "dhūmrā ca" and "surottama.
2. Therein, he defines the first [type of] earth, the "excellent lotus-like" (supadmā), with the verse beginning with "candana," etc.
3. He characterizes the second, auspicious stage (*bhūmi*) with the words beginning "river," etc. (p.
"The auspicious one (*bhadra*) is proclaimed as being endowed with sacrificial trees, bulls, and fields."
Abounding in *vakula* and *aśoka* trees, as well as with *plakṣa*, *āmra*, and *lohitaka*.
That which is entwined by *mādhavī* creepers, and that which is surrounded by *mudga*, *niṣpāva*, and *kodrava* grains,
as well as by awned grains (*śūkadhānya*) and *punnāga* trees, and that which is situated on the side of a mountain.
That which is celebrated as being full even with a very small amount of water,
and which is surrounded on all sides by groves of *bilva*, *arka*, *snuhi*, and *pīlu* trees; (7)
It was stony and hard, filled with thorny trees,
and crowded with flocks of vultures, jackals, crows, and hawks.
That [place] is proclaimed as "smoky"; one should carefully avoid it.
Then, having understood this, one should examine the ground for an auspicious site that slopes toward the east and north.

5. He characterizes the third full stage (*bhūmi*) with the verse beginning "vakula," etc. [The word] "lohitaiḥ" means with red sandalwoods or red *śobhāñjana* trees; here the instrumental case is used in the sense of indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for both this world and the next. "Niṣpāva" is a white pulse (*śimbidhānya*).
"Kodrava" is a type of grain; as Amara states: "Koradūṣa, however, is kodrava. "Punnāga" is well-known by its own name.
A tree characterized primarily by its flowers.
7. The fourth [verse], beginning with "vilvārka," indicates the smoky-colored ground. The *pīlu* is a tree well-known in the Gurjara country, called the "molasses-fruit" tree.

9. Now, the examination of the site (*bhūmiparīkṣā*) is described by the words "then" (*tataḥ*) and so forth. Having disregarded a censured site according to the method previously stated, and having identified a commendable one as worthy of acceptance, if that site passes the examination in the sequence to be described, then one should take it; otherwise, one should avoid it—this is the meaning.
(25) Thus, it is free from distress, overflowing with the waters of the *chanda-kalpa*, and flooded by them.
When the pit has been filled, [he should take] auspicious soil that remains in excess.
In that [place], a color like safflower does not fade;
likewise, a lamp does not go out, and water does not quickly perish.

10. "Unconstricted" means having ample space. "Desirable" (chandām) means being perceived as a means for achieving what is wished for. Regarding the phrase "being filled": this has been clarified in the first chapter of the *Viśvakarmaprakāśa*:
"One should dig a pit one cubit deep, and then fill it once again with that same [earth]."

By the statement, "Excessive soil [indicates] superior, middling, or inferior [ground], while deficient [soil indicates] middling or inferior respectively," and by the statement in the fourth chapter of the *Mayamata*: "When the excavated pit is filled with earth, equality is considered middling; the ground is excellent when there is an excess of earth, and inferior when there is a deficiency of earth."

11. Regarding "kusumbha": the method for this examination is stated in the *Saurakāṇḍa*: "One should place flowers of colors similar to those [of the gems] in a pit. At nightfall, as before, one should observe them at sunrise.
That color whose flower does not wither will be auspicious for that [gem]. In this regard—

It should be understood that according to the twelve-verse chapter beginning with "white, reddish" (*śvetāruṇa*), which describes the distinctions of colors such as white pertaining to the Brāhmaṇas and other castes, when flowers of those respective colors— white, red, yellow, and black— are placed in a pit,
the ground where the fading of the color of a particular flower does not occur is to be known as the most excellent for that specific color.

The mention of "resembling safflower" (*kusumbha*) should be understood as referring to the construction of palaces, since such structures are generally seen to be built by Kṣatriyas. Regarding the phrase "it does not go out": the sequence for this examination is given in the *Saurakāṇḍa*: "One should place an unbaked vessel within the mouth of a jar situated inside a pit, [filling it] with cow's..."

Having filled [the vessel] with the oblation (*havis*) as before, one should fashion the wick (*varti*). Then, according to the sequence starting from the east, one should observe the flame. That direction in which the vessel breaks or where the wick perishes is not auspicious for that person; however, that direction in which it blazes is indeed auspicious. Where it blazes in every way, it grants all desires. This will be demonstrated here. In this regard:

"Bestowing all desires" (*sarvakāmapradā*) means bestowing the desires of all. Therefore, if the flame of the lamp is bright toward the east, that site is auspicious for a Brāhmaṇa; if the flame is likewise [bright] toward the south and other directions, it is for a Kṣatriya and so forth; and if the flames are equal in all directions, that site is auspicious for all social classes (*varṇas*).

The Smārta Bhaṭṭācāryas [state]: "Water," etc. This method of examination as well will be clarified in the Saura-kāṇḍa: "At twilight, having filled a pit with water, at sunrise the wise Guru should carefully observe it to determine whether it is excellent, inferior, or middling."

White, reddish, yellow, and black [reddish-yellow, yellow, and reddish-black, according to variants k, g] are praised for the Brahmins and the other castes respectively; and that which possesses a scent equal to clarified butter, blood, fragrance, and wine [is also recommended]. (12)
Sweet, astringent, sour, and pungent—just so, it flows covered by *kuśa*, *kāśa*, *śara*, and *dūrvā* grasses. (13)
Then, under an auspicious lunar mansion, he should perform the consecration of the ground, extending as far as the boundary of the walls; thereafter, he should offer a bali-oblation to the spirits.

"If the earth remains in water, it is excellent; if it is muddy, it is middling; if it is dry and cracked, it is inferior; such ground should indeed be avoided with effort"—by this [verse], he describes the classification of the earth according to its color, beginning with "white": white for Brāhmaṇas, red...

The meaning is that [the color] is yellow for Kṣatriyas, black for Vaiśyas, and dark for Śūdras. Regarding the phrase "butter-smelling" (*ājyāmr̥giti*)—here too, the term "for Brāhmaṇas and so forth" is to be connected [to the following], because of the specific observation: "The queen should have the scent of ghee; she who has the scent of blood [should be a Kṣatriya]; the Vaiśya should have the scent of alkaline matter; and the Śūdra should have the scent of wine" (Aparārka 2).

13. Regarding "sweet" (*madhura*)—here too, the phrase "of the Brahmins and others" (*viprādīnām*) is to be supplied. As it is said in the *Viśvaprakāśa* (2): "The sweet soil is considered Brāhmaṇī; the astringent is held to be Kṣatriyā; the sour soil shall be Vaiśyā; and the pungent is considered Śūdrī," such is the observation regarding the distinction of tastes. Regarding "with *kuśa* grasses"—here too, it should be understood that "of the Brahmins and others" applies; [this refers to] with *kuśa* grasses in the *Saurakaṇḍa*.

"O sinless one, that ground which is endowed with *śrī*, *kāśa*, and *dūrvā* grasses is praised here according to the sequence beginning with the Brahmins. This is because of such a scriptural observation (*darśana*). However, the detailed examination of the characteristics of the ground (*bhūmi-lakṣaṇa-parīkṣā*) and so forth is to be found in the second chapter of the *Saura-kāṇḍa*.
14. Regarding the acquisition of that ground which has been thus recognized as excellent through examination, he says: "In that [ground]...

Here, the term *nakṣatra* is indicative of an auspicious day prescribed by the ritual manuals (*kalpa*). Likewise: "In an auspicious lunar mansion endowed with a holy lunar day (*puṇyatithi*), in a favorable *karaṇa*, at a good *lagna*, and at a moment (*muhūrta*) desired by the wise" (Mayamata 4.8).
Because of the injunctions for the consideration of lunar days and so forth in such passages as these;
27) [māṣaṃ (māṣaṃ kh, g; māṃsaṃ k)] and turmeric powder, together with parched grain [salājā (k)].
Having offered the *bhūtabali* with these— rice with lentils, curd, and parched grain— one should [offer] the thread with the eight-syllable mantra. || 15 ||
Having driven them in, one should then plant stakes in the eight directions [to ward off] those Rākṣasas and Bhūtas who dwell upon this earth. (16)
15–16 | It was previously stated that one should offer the *bhūtabali*; now he describes its ritual procedures, beginning with the word "māṣam. Regarding the *sūtra*:

"One should utter the *tāra* (Oṃ) and the word *namaḥ*, followed by the letters *na* and *ra* joined with the long [vowels *ā* and *ī*]. This supreme mantra, consisting of eight syllables, is called *pavana*. Thus, according to the authority of the *Tantrasāra*, [the mantra begins with] *oṃ namaḥ*.

The meaning is that, having cast a thread with the eight-syllable mantra "Nārāyaṇāya" for the purpose of determining the boundary for the placement of the stakes (śaṅku) as will be described, one should place eight stakes. This is indicated by the passage in the third chapter of the Saurakāṇḍa concerning the stakes: "Having established [the stakes] in the corners starting from Īśāna according to the rule by the wise... and so forth.

The installation of four pegs (śaṅku) will now be described; the practical procedure is likewise the same. It should be understood that the instruction "one should fix eight pegs" here refers to the suspicion of breaking the thread (sūtra), as it is stated in the *Mātsya Purāṇa*: "In the case of breaking the thread, death occurs; if the peg is facing downward, disease [ensues]. This applies to a wide area.

For when only four stakes have been driven in, it is entirely possible for the long thread stretched across them to break, or for the thread to slip from the stake due to its being pulled; therefore, Bhojadeva, having stated that one should examine and fix eight stakes according to the rule, says that when the thread being fixed [is disturbed], the stake [should be adjusted] in some way.

If [the thread] breaks, one should know that it portends the death of a son; if it is cut, it leads to the death of oneself or one's master. Therefore, effort must be exerted as long as the thread is being stretched out. (Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra 23.25 + 7–72).

By such statements, the driving in of the stakes and the laying of the foundation stones is intended for the purpose of avoiding the breaking of the thread and other such events which are followed by powerful misfortunes.

And he gave instruction on the effort [to be applied]. Thus, where the ground is not so extensive, the setting up of four stakes does not constitute a fault; but where there is extensiveness, the placement of eight stakes alone is correct for the purpose of dispelling doubts such as the breaking of the thread, and so it was resolved.

There is a mutual contradiction. Or rather, "eight stakes" refers to the subject of the sun as stated in the *Saurakāṇḍa*. In this *Saurakāṇḍa*, having introduced the rule, "One should fix a stake at that place and also stretch a cord from it," the stakes are recorded as being produced from trees possessing the essence suitable for sacrifice (*yajñīya-sāra*), with a width of twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).

Because of this statement, stakes (*śaṅku*) measuring twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) should be made from sacrificial wood such as *uḍumbara* and others. The details here are to be seen in the third chapter of the *Saurakāṇḍa*. Regarding that, he states the mantra for the prayer: "And the Rākṣasas... and so forth.
"May they all depart; I shall prepare a place for Hari.
Having thus addressed the spirits and other beings, he [prepared] that ground.
One should purify it. || 17 ||

Then, according to the procedure ending with clarified butter (*ājya*), one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) for the planets beginning with the Sun, together with the world-protectors (*lokapāla*). Thereafter,

18 | He states the sequence for purifying the ground with the verse beginning "āditya...". This appears to be more excellent.

[Verse 20: Regarding the plowing of the land, he says "two bulls. "Two tawny ones" is the primary rule; in their absence, "two of the same color. "Born from the *asan* tree" means originating from the *sarja* tree.

Here, the *praṇava* (Oṃ) is the heart-mantra; it is proclaimed as "to the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva. In the principal Vaiṣṇava tantra, this mantra is known as the "celestial tree" (*surapādapa*).

Thus ends the sixth chapter, on the Purification of the Elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), in the *Ādikāṇḍa* of the *Hayaśīrṣa Mahāpañcarātra*, the twelve-thousand-verse [tantra].
The total number of verses from the beginning is 127.
Regarding the phrase *samarddhena*: here, the reading *sammarddanaiḥ* as maintained in the *Vaidikasarvasva* appears to be more correct;

It is considered [as follows]: "seeds of virtue" (*śubhabīja*). Having stated that one should sow all seeds in a field ploughed by a plow, it is said:

"Rice (*vrīhi*), *śāli* rice, mung beans (*mudga*), wheat (*godhūma*), mustard (*sarṣapa*), sesame (*tila*), barley (*yava*), and medicinal herbs (*oṣadhi*)—these seven are indeed all the seeds" (*Viṣṇu Purāṇa* 2.65).
