"At the time of fruition": when the time for fruition has arrived, one should cause the herd of cows (*gokula*) to dwell there; "then that earth becomes completely pure after three days and nights"—this is because of the agreement with the third chapter of the *Saurakāṇḍa*.
23. Regarding the word "again" (*punar*): first comes the plowing of the ground, and thereafter [the removal of] clods of earth and so forth produced by the power of that plowing.

The sequence of operations is as follows: leveling by means of trampling, sowing the seed therein, and when the fruits produced from the sown seeds have been eaten by cattle wandering there, the plowing of that ground again and its leveling once more. "To the house" (gṛham) means "he should go."
Chapter Seven (The Characteristics of the Hand and the Characteristics of the Śaṅku)
The auspicious characteristics of the hand are taught for the purpose of distinguishing between measures of honor and dishonor,
because they are the most important among all ritual acts.
Listen to me. || 1 ||

A *rathareṇu* (chariot-dust) is proclaimed to consist of exactly eight *paramāṇus* (atoms); an *trasareṇu* (sunbeam-dust) is proclaimed to consist of exactly eight *rathareṇus*. In the previous chapter it was stated that one should place the *śaṅku* (gnomon) in the eight directions, and in the eighth chapter, [it is stated] in the center.
By the passage beginning with "a firmly fixed peg" (*sunishcalam shankum*), the installation of the pegs will be described.

These pegs, as well as others to be mentioned hereafter—such as temples, images, banners, flags, arches, sacrificial pits, and mandalas—are all auxiliary components of the primary ritual action; they are finite in measure and thus dependent upon the knowledge of their proportions.

The subject matter to be explained is the essential nature of measurement (*parimāṇa*). In this regard, since it is observed that all the rites under discussion are successfully accomplished by means of hand-measurements (*hasta-parimāṇa*) characterized as one, two, three, and so forth, and because the hand-measurement alone holds primacy in every case, the author begins to explain that very point with the words "measurement, weighing," and so on.

*Māna* is common measurement, while *unmāna* is vertical measurement. Since *unmāna* is mentioned immediately after *māna* here, by the term *māna* one should understand a relative smaller measurement.
Thus, for example, a chariot-dust (*rathareṇu*) has a vertical measurement in relation to an atom (*paramāṇu*), and in relation to that [chariot-dust],...

A *trasareṇu* is a unit of upward measurement (*ūrdhvaparimāṇa*). Thus, in order to indicate that a measurement of two cubits, three cubits, and so forth—relative to the measure of a single cubit—is a form of "upward measurement" (*unmāna*), he says: "measurement and upward measurement" (*mānonmāna*).
Bhojadeva also states: "The ground is the cause and the support for all structures and for all ritual actions."

"This is the sole basis for determining the divisions of measurement and so forth, since from this [text] arise these distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior types according to the circumference, height, and width of the lengths; by knowing which, one is no longer deluded. (Samarāṅgaṇa 9.11–12).
By such statements as these, he says precisely this.
2. Regarding "paramāṇu": the mention of the measurement starting from the atom (*paramāṇu*) is solely for the purpose of making known the measurement of the cubit (*hasta*).
Regarding "trasareṇu"—in this system, one *trasareṇu* consists of sixty-four atoms (*paramāṇu*). However, some [hold that] (p.
Eight of those [vālāgras] make one *likṣā*;
eight of those are known as one *yūkā*, and eight of those constitute one *yavamadhya*.
Eight barley grains shall constitute one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*); twenty-four fingers make one cubit (*kara*).
Another cubit, measuring twenty-four fingers, is likewise measured by one's own thumb.

One's own hand joined with four fingers is the "lotus-handed" (*padmahastaka*). By the passage beginning with "when the sun has entered through a lattice," they describe the substance *trasareṇu* as consisting of six atoms (or three *dvyaṇukas*). Bhojadeva, however, [identifies] the atom (*paramāṇu*) with the *rathareṇu*.
Without accepting the *trasareṇu*, [the author] states that eight *reṇus* constitute a *bālāgra* (Samarāṅgaṇa 9.4).
However, in the *Mayamata*, he states that eight *paramāṇus* constitute a *rathareṇu*, and eight of those constitute a *bālāgra*;
yet he did not mention the measurement of the *trasareṇu* as accepted by the *Hayaśīrṣa*. Thus...
In the determination of measurement, other varieties of types are also observed.

4. Regarding "aṅgula": the word *aṅgula* signifies a finger, a hand, or a foot; it is masculine when referring to these, but in the present context, it is neuter when denoting a measurement of eight barley-corns (*yava*). As it is said: "An *aṅgula* is eight times a barley-corn" (Mayūkha 5.4).

And because of the statement by Bhāskarācārya: "From the sight [of the grain], [the finger] consists of eight barley-grains (yava) in number. Therefore, the masculine reading found in the *kh* and *g* manuscripts has not been included here in the root text. Regarding the word "twenty-four": here, Bhojadeva says:
"Now, the definition of that cubit (*hasta*) in its threefold variety, together with its complete determination, is being told."

By the phrase "as shown in the Śāstra" (*samarā 9 | 3*), the threefold nature of the cubit (*hasta*) measurement is stated. That threefold nature has been demonstrated by that very same [text]: "Measured by eight barley-corns as its *aṅgula* units, and extended to the maximum length, that is called the 'superior' (*jyeṣṭha*) cubit, designated by the learned as *prāśaya*. Furthermore, that which is fashioned..."
"By those who know [the matter], that middle *hasta*—measured here by seven *aṅgulas* each consisting of seven barley-corns—is remembered as the 'common' (*sādhāraṇa*).

(2) Since it is said that 'mātra' means small, and since a *hasta* is called a 'resting place' (*śaya*), therefore that *hasta* which measures six barley-corns in length would be the 'resting place of the measure' (*mātrāśaya*). (3)" (Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra 9.28–32). Here too, it is exactly the same.
Stating the threefold measurement of the *hasta*, he first describes one measure of the *hasta* established through the sequence beginning with the *paramāṇu* as previously mentioned:
"A *kara* consists of twenty-four *aṅgulas*. [He then describes another] by not accepting the sequence beginning with the *paramāṇu*, but rather [measuring] by means of one's own thumb.
He states that the second measurement of the cubit is limited by the number twenty-four: "twenty-four.
With these cubits, one should construct a temple or a sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*).
The Sacrificial Fire [kh, g] || 5 ||
An image or a pedestal, a sacrificial pit, a mandala, as well as an archway, a banner, and a vessel endowed with excellent qualities. || 6 ||
Those who desire to attain the fruit [of their actions] should never perform [the rite] with wood that is devoid of dignity;
rather, one should take a praiseworthy piece of wood that is full of essence, such as khadira and other similar types. (7)
Having had that wood fashioned into a square by a craftsman, the wise man should make it circular, level with the ground, free from blemishes, and perfectly smooth.

5 | He states the third measurement of the cubit (*hasta*) as being measured by one's own hand plus four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*), using the words "four finger-breadths" (*caturaṅgula*). For this very reason, the plural number used in the upcoming phrase "by these cubits" (*etair hastaiḥ*) is justified.

Regarding the determination of which wood is prescribed or prohibited for the purpose of measuring the cubit here, he has already done so [earlier]: *khadira*, *añjana*, bamboo (*vaṃśa*), and so forth.
"Smooth, hard, and pleasing to the mind, and possessing core strength—such wood is desired for the fashioning of the *hasta* (the measuring instrument).
Wood that is knotted, light, burnt, decayed, cracked, unstable, or infested with hollows is not fit for the *hasta*. (Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra 9.11–12). Thus, by these two [verses].
7. Now, he begins to describe the method for fashioning the sacrificial peg (*śaṅku*) with the words "praśastaṃ" and so forth.

Here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), those trees mentioned in [Mayamata 6.6]—namely, "Tooth-wood (*danta*), sandalwood (*candana*), *khadira*, *kadara*, *śamī*, *śāka*, and *tinduka*—are to be understood as the materials to be taken.

8. Having caused a piece of wood to be made square, one should then make it circular; this is the meaning. First making it square and subsequently making it circular is solely for the sake of convenience in measuring its diameter (*vyāsa*).
"Without blemish" (*nirvraṇa*) means uninjured. "Well-proportioned" (*suṣama*) means free from defects such as unevenness from the base to the tip.
Twelve finger-breadths in length, one joint is said to be one finger-breadth;
at its base, its circumference is six finger-breadths according to its own measurement.
[The measurement] according to the span of the arms (vyāma) is [as follows]. || 9 ||
The tip should be made shorter than the base by a short measure, being only the size of a barley grain;
one should make the base equal to the width of the ground, and the tip well-proportioned.
Thus has the characteristic of the gnomon been described in due order;
having thus prepared the gnomon, the Guru should perform the determination of the directions.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, on the characteristics of the *śaṅkula*, in the Ādikāṇḍa of the *Hayaśīrṣa Mahāpañcarātra* in twelve thousand verses. || 7 ||

The total number of verses from the beginning is 138. [Verses] 9–10 state the measurement of the length of this śaṅku (gnomon) with the words "twelve," etc. That which was previously stated—"an aṅgula should consist of eight barley-corns"—does not apply here; rather, the measurement of the aṅgula here is distinct. To the question "What is it?", he says:
The word *parva* means that here the measurement of a finger (*aṅgula*) is to be understood as being by the joint at the tip of the thumb alone.

By these twelve thumb-joints, one *aratni* measurement is formed; therefore, the excellence of the gnomon (*śaṅku*) being of the measure of an *aratni*, which was stated in the *Mayamata* in the passage beginning with "the length is one *aratni*," applies here as well.

By stating that its measurement consists of twelve joints, that very point has been indicated. Regarding "at the base": the circumference of the gnomon (śaṅku) is six finger-breadths at the base and only the measure of a barley-corn at the tip. "Shorter and shorter than its own measure" means that, according to the stated proportions, there is a gradual decrease in width from the base to the tip such that—
The meaning is that the root and the tip should be well-proportioned and not marred by defects such as being uneven or jagged.

Regarding "on the ground": there are three types of size—the superior measure is one *aratni* (the measure of twelve thumb-joints), the middling measure is eighteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), and the inferior measure is twelve finger-breadths.

The measurement of the gnomon is as follows. In that regard, it is stated by the phrase "equal to the excavation of the ground" (bhūmicchedasamam) that the proportional gradation of the gnomon's measurement should be made according to the proportional gradation of the width of the site-ground.
11. The meaning is that one should perform the determination of the directions according to the sequence to be described hereafter.
The Eighth Chapter:
(The Determination of Directions, Knowledge of Vital Points, Knowledge of Protrusions, and the Mandala of the Site)
The Blessed One said:
Having made the external ground level, one should fashion it into a square on all sides;
having made the earth even like water, resembling the surface of a mirror.

1 | Having explained the procedure for constructing the ritual peg (*śaṅku*) in the previous chapter, [it is stated]: "If one should act according to what is seen [without knowing the directions], one who has failed will go to hell; the preceptor (*deśika*) should perform the rites after having ascertained the directions by the movement of the sun. According to this statement cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, [the rites] for the temple and so forth must be performed immediately after the knowledge of the directions.

"Where, indeed, the irregularity of the site is not properly understood, there one should determine the orientation of the pure directions by fixing a peg. According to this authority stated in that very [text], one should establish the direction here as well by means of a peg,
in accordance with what will be said subsequently regarding the construction of that peg.
He explains the method for determining the directions with the words beginning "external" (*vāhya*) and so forth. A site (*vāstu*) consists of two parts:

the external and the internal. Among these, that part which is situated outside and contiguous to the temple, the four-hall house (*catuḥśālā*), or other such structures, is the external; and that which falls within them is the internal. Here...
Since both of these parts are equal, [the author] says "bāhya" (external) in order to demonstrate the procedure that will be described:

the meaning is that one should make a square equal to the external site on all four sides of the ground intended as the *vāstu*. Regarding "bhūmim" (the ground): one should make that square ground level with water (*toyasamām*).

The meaning is "having performed [the following]. For it is stated [in the *Mayamata*] that the leveling of the ground is accomplished by means of water: "Having leveled the surface of the earth within the seized site, one should make it even and square with water to the depth of a *daṇḍa*" (*Mayamata* 6.2–3). In this statement from the *Mayamata*, the phrase "to the depth of a *daṇḍa*" is used.

In this case as well, the method of leveling should be understood as follows: having leveled the ground and constructed a dam made of earth and other materials all around, one fills the interior with water; then, having placed a certain measured staff here and there around it at intervals, [the level is determined] by the quantity of that water corresponding to the measurement of those staffs.

One should examine whether that ground is level, uneven, or slants toward the directions. If it is uneven, one should make it level by this very same method. Regarding the term "like a mirror"—the meaning is that it is as smooth as the surface of a mirror's belly.
The phrase "level like water" is intended to dispel any suspicion of slanting toward the directions. The expression "resembling the belly of a mirror" applies everywhere.
To avoid defects such as unevenness and the like,
one should rotate eight circles, each measuring twelve finger-breadths in size.
Having fixed a perfectly steady gnomon in the center, one should observe its shadow.

2. Regarding what is to be done once the ground has been leveled in this manner, he says "twelve" and so forth. Having drawn a circle on this perfectly level surface by means of rotation, one should place a twelve-finger-long gnomon (śaṅku) at its center. By following the succession of the shadow at the tip [of the gnomon] upon the circle, one should mark two points—the eastern and western—corresponding to the forenoon and afternoon.
One should stand facing that [mandala]. Then, by means of a perfectly equal rotation, one should again draw two circles.

When the junctions produced by the union of those two are situated to the south and north of the center, one should place a thread between the two junctions running east-west, and another in the middle running north-south. By means of the tips of those threads, one should determine the directions starting from the east. Thus it is said.

According to the statement cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa in the *Prāṇatoṣiṇī*, one first draws a circle on the ground; then, in its center, a gnomon (*śaṅku*) is erected. In the forenoon, when the shadow-tip of the gnomon—which hangs over the direction toward the west—is determined, and in the afternoon, when it hangs over the east, two circles are drawn at those respective points to preserve the marks.

By rotating [the instrument] equally in both directions, two further circles are drawn— one to the south and one to the north of the central point within the first circle— in order to preserve those respective marks; thus, by means of the shadow, after determining the cardinal directions, those marks are established in their proper places in due order.

The construction of four circles has been previously described. However, here, by the instruction "one should rotate eight circles," once the construction of the eight circles has first been performed, there is still no determination of the cardinal directions at that time;
consequently, because the placement of the circles is arbitrary, it is possible that the falling of the gnomon-shadow (śaṅkucchāyā) may also be arbitrary.

If these circles were used for determining the directions, it would not be possible; rather, they would simply be useless, which would result in a great inconsistency. Therefore, following the authoritative method shown earlier by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, this text is explained by us as follows: having drawn a certain circle at sunrise in the morning.

Having fixed a perfectly immovable gnomon in the center of that [circle] and observed its shadow, and having so observed, one should draw a single circle twelve finger-breadths in diameter toward the west using a thread aligned with that shadow. Likewise, when the sun has moved toward the west and the shadow of the gnomon begins to move toward the east, one should do the same toward the east.
One should fashion a single circle twelve finger-breadths in diameter using a straight thread;
upon its entry and exit, one should observe the shadow of the gnomon upon it.
By means of the two marks at the tips of the gnomon’s shadow, one should determine the east and west directions. || 3 ||
When the sun has moved toward the east or the west, one should determine the north and south;
when the sky is clear at the equinox, one should determine the direction by means of a gnomon.

3. Regarding that, he states a specific detail in the sequence of determining the shadow (*chāyā*), beginning with the word "entry" (*praveśa*). The meaning is that the determination of the shadow must be performed during entry and exit upon that ground.
Here, [it is determined] by the verse beginning: "If the shadow in the forenoon or afternoon enters within that circle... (*mayā* 6.8).

In the forenoon and afternoon, the determination of direction was described by means of the solar shadow entering within the circle; here too, by the terms "entry" and "exit," he expresses essentially that same method. Therein, "entry" refers to the morning at sunrise, when the shadow of the gnomon falls toward the west.
Then, as the sun ascends further upward, that shadow becomes increasingly longer;

when it gradually diminishes in length and enters its own location at a distance of no less than twelve *aṅgulas* from the center of the circle, then its tip [should be marked] along the line coinciding with the central point of that circle.

The meaning is that one should understand it as facing west. Regarding "niṣkrama" (exit)—in this manner, the eastern direction is to be determined at the time of exit. For instance, when the sun has ascended to midday and is hanging over the western quarter, the shadow of the gnomon moving toward the east gradually attains length. In that case—

Having first constructed a single circle measuring twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) with its center at the eastward mark according to the previously mentioned westward sequence, one should determine the west by means of the eastern point on its circumference; it is in order to teach this method of determining the directions that he says "by means of the two marks of the tips of the shadow of the gnomon. [The lines] of the shadows of the gnomon run from east to west.

By means of the two primary marks, one should establish and determine the east and west directions for the entry and exit according to the sequence previously stated; this is the meaning. Furthermore, circles should be drawn here and there so that even those measuring twelve finger-breadths may find their place through mutual contact.

4 | Thus, the method for determining the eastern and western directions has been stated. Now, as to what the means for determining the southern and northern directions is, he says "prāk" (eastward) and so forth. Rāghavabhaṭṭa taught the determination of the southern and northern directions by means of dropping a plumb-line and the drawing of a circle for the purpose of establishing various marks in their respective places; here, however, he explains that in a different manner.

For instance, when the sun has moved to the east or west and has reached the equinox, situated upon the equatorial line connecting the eastern and western points, one should establish—that is, determine—the northern and southern directions.
In this manner, during autumn and spring, one should determine the direction from the sun.
One should determine the east by the piercing of Puṣya, or by the interval between Citrā and Svātī;
one should determine the north by the piercing of Dhruva, using the middle conjunction.
Having taken a square stone or a very beautiful brick—

one should attend to this point here: by the statement "one should rotate eight circles," [the procedure is] by rotating to the left from the two previously made circles of twelve finger-breadths each, one in front and one behind.
One should draw three circles joined together measuring twelve finger-breadths on the right side, and likewise three circles on the left;

thus there are eight circles—four situated at the cardinal directions and four situated at the intermediate corners. Among these, the northern half of the eastern circle is the northeastern circle, and the eastern half of the northern circle is likewise [the southeastern circle].
Having determined the western semicircle and the northern semicircle, as well as the northern semicircle and the western semicircle,
one should recognize the northern junction at twenty-four finger-breadths from both sides; likewise, in determining the southern direction,
[one proceeds] with the eastern semicircle and the southeastern semicircle, and the southern semicircle and the northeastern semicircle.

Having determined the western half of the northern circle, the southern circle, and the western half of the southern circle, one should understand that the middle point of the central circle lies toward the south, at a junction of twenty-four finger-breadths from both sides as before; this is the resulting conclusion. And then, when the sun has moved to the east or west—

By this, it is shown that the determination of the south and north directions is in accordance with the *Hayaśīrṣa* [Purāṇa], being based precisely upon the previously well-determined east and west; however, the instruction on determining the directions by means of the falling of the eight circles is for the purpose of defining the cardinal and intermediate points. He states that all these aforementioned methods for ascertaining the directions apply only to the equinox.

Regarding the term *viṣuva*: it is precisely at the equinox (*viṣuva*) that the east and west points lie on the same meridian due to the movement of the sun; therefore, it is only there that the determination of the directions by means of the gnomon and other such methods is possible. (5) Now, one might ask: "What is this so-called equinox, where the determination of direction is thus established? To this he says: "autumn," etc. And this...
This refers specifically to the autumn and spring seasons; the meaning is that it is precisely during the months of Āśvina and Caitra that the sun reaches the equatorial line (viṣuvarekhā).
6. Having thus described the procedure for determining the directions by day, he now states [the method] for the night, beginning with "But the east... [and mentioning] Kṛttikā.

"The space between Śravaṇā, Puṣyā, Citrā, and Svāti is the form of the eastern direction when [the sun] has risen to the extent of a yoke. By this [statement from the *Prāṇāgnihotra*], the east is defined at the rising of Śravaṇā; likewise, at the rising of Kṛttikā;
and by the statement from the *Trikāṇḍamaṇḍala* cited in that very same work—"between Citrā and Svāti are the moon and the sun"—it is established regarding the night.

The sequence for determining the directions by observing the positions of the stars has been shown; here, with the words "the eastern direction" and so forth, he describes that very same sequence. At night, when Karkaṭa has risen, one should determine the eastern direction by piercing [the sky] at Puṣya;
or, when Kanyā has risen, immediately after the rising of Citrā, one should determine it by the rising of Svāti, or by the middle point between them, through that piercing.
It should also be understood that one should establish the western direction.
Having established [the points] in the four directions, one should then cause the marks for the threads to be made. (p. 38) || 7 ||
Having thus made the marks for the threads,
one should feed twelve eminent Brahmins there with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), being composed and devoted to Viṣṇu.
After this, for the sake of pleasing the lords of the months, there should be the laying out of the lines;
one should then be diligent in order to gain knowledge of the major and minor vital points (marmas) and so forth. 9.
By means of observations, recitations, sounds, and the movements of the sacrificer;
"by piercing the pole star at night" refers to the determination of the north, meaning because the pole star rises in the north.
Likewise, by means of the middle conjunction, one should raise the north and the south through the opening between the east and west which has been determined; this is the meaning.

7. Having thus determined the directions, he states the sequence for establishing their dimensions with the words "caturasrām" (square). The form "gṛhya" uses the *yap* substitution for the suffix *ktvā*, which is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*). Regarding the word "vā" (or): by this word it is indicated that where a temple is to be constructed out of stone, one should take a stone, and where it is to be made of brick, one should take a brick; this is stated in the eleventh chapter, the *Śilādhivāsana-paṭala*.

The placement of bricks (*iṣṭakā-nyāsa*) must be performed in a temple made of brick; in one made of stone, the placement of stones (*śilā-vinyāsa*); and in one made of gravel, the placement of gravel (*karkara-maya*), as will be stated later. Furthermore, there is no authority for deviating from this sequence here unless there is a specific obstacle. The phrase "in the four directions" means on the ground of the site (*vāstu-bhūmi*).

9. Now, following the determination of the directions, regarding the ascertainment of the nature of the Vāstupuruṣa which is to be performed, [the author] explains the knowledge of his vital points (*marman*), since ignorance of them results in undesirable consequences. In this regard:
"This person has the east and north as his head; he is face-downward, and the Fire-god (*Śikhin*) is upon his head" (Bṛhat-saṃhitā 52.51).

The laying out of the sixty-four squares (*catuḥṣaṣṭipadanyāsa*) must be performed upon the various limbs of the Vāstupuruṣa as described by these [verses], according to the sequence to be explained hereafter, so that the respective deities of those limbs may be properly established in their corresponding squares. And those squares are to be accomplished by the casting of lines (*sūtrapāta*). Now, regarding these lines:
The intersections of lines running from corner to corner, as well as the equal centers of the squares, are the vital points (*marmāṇi*).

For example: the intersections of the bamboo-lines and those centers of the squares which are equal—these one should know to be the vital points; a wise man should not cause them to be afflicted. If they are afflicted by impure vessels, stakes, pillars, and the like, [the house will suffer].

And by means of arrows, they inflict pain upon the limbs of the householder that correspond [to those parts]. (Bṛhat Saṃhitā 52.57–58). By such passages, the nature of the *marmans* and the possibility of undesirable consequences arising from their affliction have been described. Bhojadeva also [states this] on page 39.
The wise man should examine the location of the thorn (or flaw) within the body of the site accordingly.
"By leaping, by the sight of the thread, and by the utterance of names;

those who are the thirteen internal deities and those who are the thirty-two external ones—their locations, their vital points (*marmāṇi*), their veins, and the bamboo-like channels within them. (Samarāṅgaṇa 13.6). Having thus described the vital points (*marmāṇi*) with this [verse], [the text proceeds] regarding them...

A twofold division is accepted based on the distinction between major *marmas* and minor *marmas*. Among these, the major *marmas* are stated as follows: "The six major *marmas* of this person, who is like a dwelling, are said to be in the mouth, the heart, the navel, the head, and likewise in the two breasts. As for the minor *marmas*, however, they are those veins (*sirās*) which exist in all four directions across all four divisions; these are the [minor] *marmas*.
Having stated, "And those situated in the middle of the door [are forbidden]" (*Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra* 13.7–10), [the text continues]:

"They say that from the crushing of vital points (*marman*) by means of doors or even by walls, the householder suffers misfortune or even the ruin of his lineage" (*Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra* 13.12); thus, [it is taught] due to the crushing of various such limbs.
The connection with various undesirable results has been stated; however, for fear of excessive length, they are not cited here.

In ultimate reality, however, one must avoid stepping upon those specific points of the site, as well as the major vital spots (*mahāmarmas*) of its parts such as the entrance, and the secondary vital spots (*upamarmas*) such as the bamboo-joists, so that no injury may occur to them.

It should be understood that the arrangement of the doors and other features must be performed. 10. Now, concerning the ground to be avoided as described in the *Prāṇatoṣaṇī*: "A cracked site causes death; a saline (ūṣara) one destroys wealth; one with thorns (saśalyā) constantly gives rise to affliction; an uneven one brings fear from enemies. Likewise..."

At the time of commencing the construction of a palace, and especially for a house and so forth, the extraction of the *śalya* (the structural pin or obstacle) must be performed if one desires one's own welfare; otherwise, there may be the death of the master or likewise his departure to a foreign land.
One should extract the *śalya* with great effort if one desires one's own welfare. (Chapter 3)

By such statements from the *Mahākapilapañcarātra* cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa, which declare that ground defiled by a "thorn" (impurity) is followed by powerful undesirable consequences, [the author] states the method for identifying the thorn when it must be removed: "by means of observations. By means of observations (*darśanaiḥ*).
By observing false forms, colors, and so forth—such as those of women, men, animals, and the like—haphazardly within the body of the dwelling;
by recitations, meaning by calling out the names of various owners;
by sounds, meaning by hearing sounds that are unreal and similar to the cries of cats, jackals, donkeys, camels, and the like; and likewise—

"By the movements of the patron" (yajamānasya ceṣṭitaiḥ) means by the aforementioned deformities of the limbs, or by behaviors resembling those of animals. "The discerning one" (vicakṣaṇaḥ) refers to a teacher whose intellect has been purified by the study of the instructions on extracting splinters; the meaning is that such a teacher should correctly identify the splinter within the body of the site.
Then, from hearing the sound, one should diligently recognize the arrow. (11)
One should recognize that the dart of that being has been described as "seeing," "leaping over," or "proclaiming the name" by means of fasting and other such methods. (12)
One should indicate the presence of a structural defect (śalya) in the house by means of physical abnormalities in the resident. || 13 ||

11. Furthermore, he says: "Or else, because of the leaping over of the thread"—that is, because the tips of the pegs (saṅku) set up on all sides of the site for the purpose of discerning the measurements are seen to be bypassed by the thread being tied as it is cast over them.

By observing the bodies of humans, animals, and so forth, by speaking their names, by uttering the name of anyone whatsoever, and by hearing sounds belonging to the same class as the sounds of animals and the like— through such attentive and specific effort— one should know the "thorn" (the arrowhead); that is to say, one should understand, according to the method to be described, which sentient being's thorn it is.
12. Now he specifies that very [vision] by saying "darśanam" (the vision): the genitive case in "yasya" (of whom) should be understood as the objective case (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*) in every instance.

If, in this or that place, or even unexpectedly, within the dwelling or the body, a female form or a male form, or its specific details, or cattle such as cows, horses, and so forth, should be seen from time to time, then—
One should understand that the presence of various bodily parts, such as the anus and so forth, exists below that particular level. Regarding "leaping" (*laṅghanam*):

according to the method previously described, one should identify a thorn by means of an animal or the like; for instance, one should know that the thorn of whichever animal leaps over that thread is located there—just as, when it is leaped over by a cat, [the thorn belongs to] the cat.

"By a jackal [is known] the jackal; by both male and female [is known] those two," it is said. "That which is spoken"—meaning the sound that is heard—indicates that there is a thorn (foreign object) there. By hearing the cries of an owl and so forth, one should know that there is such-and-such a thorn.
"Proclaimed by name" means by repeatedly calling out names such as Devadatta or Yajñadatta.
By the phrase "that thorn of that being," he states that one should infer that the thorn of a particular person or object exists therein.
Regarding the word "should indicate": for a householder, [it is indicated] from bodily changes, such as the form of scratching or other deformities of the limbs, according to the actual site.
One should indicate the presence of a *śalya* (impurity or obstacle). Regarding the phrase "from bodily distortions" (*aṅgavikārataḥ*):

the meaning is that if, at the time of commencing the construction of a temple, a householder should experience a bodily distortion—such as itching—in a particular limb, whether it be the head, the arm, or elsewhere, one should know that there is the existence of a *śalya* in that very part of the *vāstupuruṣa*. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Prāṇatoṣaṇī*:
In the words of the *Mahākapilapañcarātra*, the extraction of a thorn— whose existence is inferred by the act of scratching according to the divisions of the limbs— is taught as follows (p.
At the time of commencing the construction of a palace, the wise man should firmly insert a "thorn" (śalya) into that part of the body of the Vāstu deity which a person touches.
If a man scratches his head, one should extract a splinter from the head;
it should be understood that a splinter exists there, even if [the pain] is felt while digging at both hands.
Fire, disease,
and loss of wealth arise wherever one extracts a thorn [or performs surgery], if one desires one's own welfare.
If, however, there is itching in the two forelegs, one should indicate an iron chain;
its measurement is two cubits, and its characteristics have been described to you.
There may be the death of the master, or likewise his departure to a foreign land;
therefore, one who desires his own welfare should extract the thorn from its location.
If the broad [part] is itching, one should diagnose a splinter of bell-metal (kāṃśya-śalya);
it remains with only one hand—thus has the symptom been described to you.
An unchaste wife brings about the loss of one's reputation;
therefore, if one desires one's own welfare, one should diligently extract this thorn.
If the hand itches while digging, one should predict a skeleton;
however, if the excavation reaches a depth of three cubits, it will be found, and not otherwise.
There may be fire, burning, disease, affliction, and even death;
therefore, one who desires their own welfare should diligently uproot this deception.
If one scratches the back, however, one should indicate the presence of an arrow in the arm;
it should remain with only one hand, of this there is no doubt.
In that case, there will be the death of the master, or the wife becomes unchaste;
however, when the foot itches, one should predict a splinter in the hand.
The characteristic you have described will persist for one and a half cubits;
it brings about the destruction of women, royal punishment, and the loss of crops.
If one desires one's own welfare, one should diligently extract the thorn;
however, if there is itching in the belly, one should indicate a stone there.
The characteristics have been described to you by the measure of two cubits;
whether an omen is seen or its sound is heard, [it is significant].
Or, one should point out the name of that person whose name is being recited as the thorn.
The wise one, pure and wearing white garments, with his limbs anointed with white sandalwood paste and adorned with all ornaments, should mark out the constituent parts of the site. (15)
A snakebite may occur there; therefore, one should extract the arrow.
If one scratches the knees, one should indicate that there is ash there;
it remains for two hand-breadths—thus has the characteristic been described to you.
"It causes fire-burns, mental anguish, afflictions, suffering, and fears;
one performs such karma as this, therefore one should indeed extract it.
Thus, by other such bodily distortions as well, it should be understood that there is a *śalya* (foreign object/pain) in various parts of the body. 14.

He clarifies what was previously stated in the verse beginning with "pūrvaṃ yaddarśanaiḥ" by means of the term "śakuna": "Even Varāhamihira has said: 'When entering a house that is half-finished or already completed, the architect and the householder should observe the omens—where he stands and which limb he touches.'"
If a bird, illuminated by the sun, cries out at that time with a human-like voice,
a bone should be indicated in that place, corresponding to the limb touched.
Or, if at the time of the omen other animals such as elephants, horses, and dogs bark in response,
then the bone originated from that [animal], being produced from its very limb.
When the thread is being stretched out, a braying like that of a donkey indicates a bone-thorn;
or, when the thread is leaped over by a dog or a jackal, a thorn should be declared.

By such passages as (Bṛhat 52.103–106), the method of the science of surgery (*śalyajñāna*) has been described for the most part in accordance with the *Hayaśīrṣa*. Up to this point, the science of surgery has been explained; however, the extraction of foreign bodies (*śalyoddhāra*) will be discussed in the tenth chapter, the section on the offering of water (*arghyadānapaṭala*).

15. Having thus explained the sequence of the knowledge of the nails (*śalyajñāna*), [the text states: "One should always employ sixty-four [divisions] in a temple (*prāsāda*) and eighty-one in a house (*gṛha*), which divide the respective parts within the body of the Vāstupuruṣa. (p. 43) 16.
He begins to describe the method of arranging the layout of the *vāstumaṇḍala* with the words "the limb of the site," and so forth.
"One should draw lines" means according to the sequence that will be described hereafter.
(16) Now, one might ask: how many squares (*pada*) should be laid out in this mandala? To this he replies: "sixty-four," and so on.

The meaning is that when constructing a palace one should make sixty-four squares, and when constructing a house, eighty-one squares. Now, after describing the threefold division of the *vāstu*, Bhojadeva states: "That which consists of eighty-one squares, that which consists of one hundred squares, and that which consists of sixty-four squares—thus the *vāstu* is declared here to be of three kinds. Having introduced this, he continues:

The wise man should divide the dwellings of the social orders, the residences of royal palaces, and the abode of Indra into eighty-one squares. Likewise, various types of temples and diverse pavilions should be measured by the intelligent one using a division of one hundred squares. Furthermore, that which consists of sixty-four squares—by that [method]...
One should divide [the site] into royal camps, villages, market towns (*kheṭa*), and so forth, as well as cities and the like, according to the method stated in *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra* 13.1.3–5.

In that manner, a division has been made for the three types of *vāstu-maṇḍalas*—beginning with the eighty-one-square grid—according to their respective domains. According to that system, the houses of the social orders (*varṇins*) and of kings belong to the domain of the eighty-one-square grid.

If it is argued that there is an unavoidable mutual contradiction— since *prāsādas* (palaces) and *maṇḍapas* (pavilions) pertain to areas of one hundred *padas*, whereas the royal camp (*rājaśibira*) and so forth pertain specifically to areas of sixty-four *padas*, and thus do not pertain to the divine abodes (*devabhavana*) according to the *Hayaśīrṣa* [Purāṇa]— it is replied: as for the *prāsādas*...

In the statement of Bhojadeva beginning with "various [types] likewise," the terms *prāsāda* (palace) and *maṇḍapa* (pavilion) refer specifically to the royal residence. With reference to the eighty-one-square grid (*ekāśītipada*), it says: "There, for the sake of the king’s installation in the place of the *maitrapada*, a palace facing east should be constructed according to rule by Pṛthivīñjaya; [it should contain] the *śrīvṛkṣa* and the *sarvatobhadra* [mandalas]."
Furthermore, there is another known as the Muktakoṇa; whatever auspiciously characterized palace a king may desire, he should have it constructed [in this style].

This is because Bhojadeva has stated that the word *prāsāda* refers specifically to a particular type of royal residence in passages such as *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra* 15.16.17; and furthermore, because he asserts that these two share the same scope by stating that the *vāstu* known as the hundred-square (*śatapada*) is produced from the eighty-one-square (*ekāśītipada*) in *Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra* 14.12.

And likewise— even though there is no difference [among them] when the status of being a royal residence (*rājabhavana*) is emphasized, these [structures] are distinct due to the division into sub-classes, such as *prāsāda*-hood and *maṇḍapa*-hood, which are defined by their respective specific characteristics and are pervaded by the property of being a royal palace (*rājagṛha*).
When the field has been made square and divided into eight parts on both sides,
one should then draw the diagonal lines; thus, the divine portions [are established].
One should fashion [the syllables] *rudra* (? *kh* and *g*. || 17 ||
It should be noted that while the royal palaces have the dimension of one hundred *pada*s, the others have the dimension of eighty-one *pada*s.

However, Bhojadeva, being intent on explaining only royal residences, cities, gardens, and so forth, asked, "What is the use of this curiosity for explaining the abodes of the gods, which are irrelevant here? and thus [described them] as having sixty-four *pada*s.

One does not commit an offense by including temples within [the category of] "interior spaces. Alternatively, since the phrase "in a city and so forth" includes temples as well under the word "etcetera," everything is without contradiction; this is the summary. Nor is there a conflict with the statement in the *Amara-kośa*, "A *prāsāda* belongs to gods and kings," regarding the rule "but [the suffix] *cha* is used for sixty-four [parts] in a *prāsāda*."

It should be stated that the term *prāsādapada* is common to both temples and royal palaces; however, according to the statement from the *Liṅgapurāṇa* cited in the *Vāstuyāgatattva*, "The sixty-four-square site-plan (*catuḥṣaṣṭipada-vāstu*) is for every temple, while the eighty-one-square site-plan (*ekāśītipada-vāstu*) grants success for human [dwellings]," the sixty-four-square plan [is prescribed].

Because it is stated that [the term] refers exclusively to temples (*devagṛha*), and because Bhojadeva’s statement— "The royal palace (*nṛpamandira*) should be laid out divided by eighty-one squares" (*Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra* 25.9)—
specifically identifies the royal residence as the subject matter for the eighty-one-square site plan, the word *prāsāda* here [refers to a temple].

The conclusion is that one must understand this as referring exclusively to the temple of the deity (*devagṛha*), and not even in a dream should it be imagined as referring to the royal palace (*rājagṛha*).

(17) Since this treatise is intended solely to refer to the temple of the deity, one should disregard the eighty-one-pada mandala— which, though mentioned, is irrelevant to the context— and instead [focus on] the relevant...

He explains the sixty-four squares: "caturasrīm" and so forth. Having first made the ground square, one should divide it eightfold on both sides. In that division, nine lines extending eastward and nine extending northward must be drawn. When this is done, there are sixty-four squares. Of these lines—

And the designations were shown by Viśvakarman. Therein, for the nine lines extending from east to west, the designations in order from the north are as follows: Śrī, Yaśomatī, Kāntā, Supriyā, Parā, Śivā, Suśobhā, Sadhanā, and the ninth is known as Ibha. These extend from east to west.
Furthermore, they are situated in sixty-four squares (*viśva* 5.22.23). In the sequence starting from the west, the names of the channels (*śirā*) flowing toward the south and north are:
Dhanyā, Dharā, Viśālā, Sthirā, Rūpā, Gadā, Niśā, Vibhavā, Prabhavā, and another, Saumyā; these are the channels resting upon both the auspicious and the inauspicious. (*Viśva*)
Śiva is to be known from half a corner; Parjanya is situated in one square (pada).
Jaya is to be known as occupying two squares, and Sureśa occupies one square. || 18 ||
Bhāskara is to be known as being in one quarter; Satya is held to occupy two quarters;
Bhṛśa is to be understood as standing in three-quarters; and Vyoman is situated in half a quarter.
Hutāśana occupies half a square, while Pūṣan is situated in one full square.
Vitatha occupies two squares, and Gṛhakṣata is known to occupy a single square.
Vaivasvata stands on one foot; Gandharva is situated on two feet. Bhṛṅga is to be known as standing on one foot, and Mṛga is situated on half a foot. || 21 ||

5 | 23 | 24) For these eighteen lines are designated by the term "veins" (*śirā*), and it has already been stated previously that they are situated within the vital points (*marman*); therefore, enough with further elaboration here. Regarding the phrase "corner line" (*koṇarekhā*): then, having constructed sixty-four squares according to the sequence previously described, one should draw one corner line in each of the four-cornered squares in succession.

The meaning is "having given. Thus, the sense is that one should draw a line in the northeast corner-square of the mandala from the northeast to the southwest; in the southeast square from the southeast to the northwest;
in the southwest square from the southwest to the northeast; and in the northwest square from the northwest to the southeast. When this has been done, [of the mandala]...
In each corner, there is one horizontal line. This is the sequence for marking the mandala. Regarding the phrase "the portions of the gods" (*surabhāgān*):
the meaning is that one should assign the portions of the gods who will be mentioned later, according to the method to be described, within those squares (*padas*).
(18) He explains the manner of that assignment from the word "Śiva" up to the end of the chapter: in the first row, in the half of the northeast corner (*īśānakoṇa*).

Śiva occupies half a square. To his south, Parjanya occupies one square. To his south, and including the square below that, Jayanta occupies two squares. Regarding the statement "Jaya, situated in the root [square], occupies two squares," here "Jaya" refers to Jayanta, because of the natural sense of the ninth chapter which states, "an oblation should be offered to Jayanta. Alternatively, as held in the *Vāstuyāgatattva*, it means "Jayanta, situated in two squares."

And because of its consistency with the statements in the *Devīpurāṇa*: "To the south of that is Sureśa (Indra), occupying one square (19). Beyond that is Bhāskara, occupying one square. To the south of that, and together with the square below it, is Satya, occupying two squares. To the south of that is Bhṛśa, occupying one square. Then, in the half-square of the southeast corner is Vyoma, occupying half a square. Thus, these eight are to be worshipped in the east."
The external deities,
the ancestors (pitṛs), and the doorkeeper (dauvārika) are to be known as occupying half [of a square] each on the pedestal.
Sugrīva is to be known as the two-footed one; indeed, Puṣpadantaka is situated alone. || 22 ||
A planet situated in the excess of the water-signs (Pisces) is indeed an Asura; one situated in two signs is a Śoṣa;
one in a single sign is known as a Śoka; and a malefic occupying half a sign is considered to be an Ardha-ga. || 23 ||
Roga is to be known as occupying half a square, while Nāga is situated in a full square;
Mukhya is to be known as occupying two squares, and Bhallāṭa is stationed in a single square. || 24 ||

20. Now, in the southern row, in the western half of the southeast corner, is Hutāśana occupying half a square. To its west is Pūṣan occupying one square. To its west, in the single northern square, is Vitatha occupying two squares. To its west is Gṛhakṣata occupying one square.
To the west of that is Vaivasvata (Yama), occupying one square. To the west of that, in the northern part of the single square, is the Gandharva, occupying two squares.
To the west of that is Bhṛṅgarāja, occupying one square. At the base, Bhṛṅga is also to be known as occupying one square;
this is because of the natural sense of the statement in the *Matsya Purāṇa* (Chapter 227): "Bhṛṅga is Bhṛṅgarāja, and the Gandharva is Bhṛṅgarāja. Then...
In the southern half of the southwest corner is Mṛga, occupying half a square. Thus are the eight deities of the southern direction. 22.

Now, in the western row, in the northern half of the southwest corner are the Pitṛs (Ancestors), occupying half a square each. To the north of them is Dauvārika, occupying one square. To the north of him is Sugrīva, occupying two squares together with the single square to his east. To the north of him is Puṣpadanta, occupying one square.

23. To the north of that is Varuṇa, occupying one square. To the north of that is Asura, occupying two squares together with the preceding single square. To the north of that is Śoṣa, occupying one square. Then, in the middle of the northwest corner, is Pāpa, occupying half a square. Regarding "Pāpa," the *Bṛhatsaṃhitā* states "Pāpayakṣma. Thus are the eight deities of the western direction.
24. Then, in the northern row, in the western half of the northwest corner, there is Roga occupying half a square. To its east is Nāga occupying one square.
Yakṣeśvara is to be known as occupying one square, while Nāgarāja is situated in two squares. (p. 47)
The great goddess Śrī is established in the foot, and Aditi is situated in half [of it]. || 25 ||
The waters are to be known as those moving on foot, for the calf of the waters stands upon its feet;
Aryaman, situated in the four-footed, should be understood as being located in the eastern middle.
Savitṛ is to be known as being in one quarter, and Sāvitrī is established in one quarter;
from that, Vivasvat is to be understood as abiding in four quarters.
To the east of that, together with Dakṣa, is the principal one, Dvipada; this is likewise stated in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā.
However, in the Devīpurāṇa as cited in the Vāstuyāgatattva, it is seen as "Viśvakarmā is indeed [the deity] on the Dvipada. To the east of that is Bhallāṭa, who occupies a single square (ekapada).

25. To the east of that is Yakṣmeśvara (Soma), occupying one square; according to the Devīpurāṇa, he is Yajñeśvara, and according to the Bṛhatsaṃhitā, he is Soma. To the east of that, together with Dakṣa, is Nāgarāja, occupying two squares. To the east of that is Śrī, occupying one square. Then, in the half of the northeast corner, is Aditi, occupying half a square. Thus are the eight deities of the northern direction.
In this sequence, thirty-two outer deities are to be worshipped eight times in each of the four directions.
Regarding such a classification of deities, one should worship the gods established on the *padas*: thirty-five in total;
thirty-two are to be worshipped externally, and thirteen are to be worshipped internally. This is precisely what is stated in the passage beginning with "O Goddess" (*devī*).
The regulator [of the arrangement].
26. Now, the deities within the words (*antaḥpada-devatā*) are described. In the second row, at the word *īśāna*, there are two one-word deities (*ekapada*).
In the third row, at the word *īśāna*, there is one one-word deity, namely *āpavatsa*. From that, [the sequence proceeds] from the two words situated between the eastern direction and the center.
From the four lower squares presided over by Śakra and Bhāskara, upwards from the station of Brahmā is Aryaman, occupying four squares (27).
Then, in the second row, in the square of Agni is Savitṛ, occupying one square. Then, in the third row, in the square of Agni...
The Sāvitrī consists of a single foot.
Indra and Indrajaya are each established separately.
Mitra stands on four feet and is situated in the west. || 28 ||
Rudra indeed stands on one foot, and Yakṣman (or Brahmā) is situated on one foot;
Dharādhara is to be known as being on four feet in the north.
He fell. || 29 ||
The four-faced Prajāpati, situated in the center, should be known as being in the fourth [enclosure];
outside, all the attendants of the deities, beginning with Skanda, are stationed.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, on the Classification of Deities, in the Ādikāṇḍa of the *Hayaśīrṣa Mahāpañcarātra*, the twelve-thousand-verse [treatise].
The total number of verses from the beginning is 168.

Then, from the two middle squares of the southern row, which are presided over by Gṛhakṣata and Yama, there are four squares above the four lower squares at the position of Brahmā, occupied by the four-footed Vivasvān.

28. Then, in the second row, Indra occupies one square in the Nairṛta position. Next, in the third row, Indrajaya occupies one square in the Nairṛta position. Then, from the two western squares presided over by Puṣpadanta and Varuṇa, Mitracatuṣpada occupies four squares below, above the station of Brahmā.

29. Then, in the second row, in the northwest square (vāyavya-pada), Rudra is one-footed. Then, in the third row, in the northwest square, Rājayakṣman is one-footed. Being worshipped in the intermediate space, Jvālākhyā, who abides in the midst of the intellect in the southwest (nairṛtya) and assumes a white form.

"He should be worshipped according to the prescribed ritual with the mantra 'mahi dyauḥ'. One should worship those external deities who have been mentioned in relation to the temple. (Viśvakarmaprakāśa 5.62–98).
This refers to the placement of colored powders (*rajas*) upon the eighty-one-square mandala established by Viśvakarman for the construction of houses and other structures.
Regarding the term "explained": in accordance with the context of the present section, it was stated that Brahman consists of nine syllables in the middle;

however, since the deities to be worshipped are for the most part identical in both the eighty-one-syllable and sixty-four-syllable systems, the colors of those respective deities are likewise the same, and thus the assignment of the *rājasa* [qualities] applies to both.

It is exactly the same. Thus, according to the sequence stated in the *Hayaśīrṣa*, when the mantras are divided into distinct deities, the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *rājasī* [mantra] should be performed according to the method described by Viśvakarman; however, the essential point is that the division of the words themselves is not to be done. Nevertheless, in the case of the placement of the deities belonging to the sixty-four-word [mantra] from the eighty-one-word [mantra], "Śikhī" becomes "Śiva," "Aditi" becomes "Śīriti," and "Diti" becomes "Aditi."
This distinction should be kept in mind.

In these statements of Viśvakarman, the arrangement of the *rajas* (colored powders) beginning from Brahmā has been described. However, for the easy understanding of the learned, we shall present that same arrangement concisely, following the order of the *Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra*.

It is demonstrated as follows: Śiva is red; Parjanya is yellow; Jayanta is yellow; Śakra is yellow; Bhāskara is red; Satya is white; Bhṛśa is black; Vyoman is black; Hutāśana (or, according to some, Vāyu) is smoky-grey; Hutāśana is red—this is the *Vaidikasārvabhauma*; Pūṣan is red; Vitatha is white.
Gṛhakṣata is drunk; (p.

Now, in order to establish that the *bali* offering is optional (*kāmya*), he says: "optional" (*kāmika*). For this very reason, the Smārta Bhaṭṭācāryas also cite the passage from the Devīpurāṇa: "Thus worshipped, the gods bestow peace and prosperity upon men; if unworshipped, they destroy both the performer and the installer. And it was further stated:

Tenth Chapter:
(The Offering of Arghya)
The Blessed Lord said: Then one should perform the worship of Vāsudeva in the place of Brahmā;
one should also perform the worship of Śrī and of the host of Hṛṣīkeśa.
Then one should perform the worship of the host of Vāsudeva with perfumes, water for the guest-offering (arghya),
flowers, food offerings (naivedya), and charming incense and lamps.
Then, one should worship upon that [altar] the Earth, the sustainer of all worlds,
beautiful in the form of a young woman, adorned with divine ornaments.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the Goddess, who is fully satisfied and has a smiling countenance;
then, having prostrated and made a request, one should contemplate her with total absorption.

1. Now, this chapter begins with the words "In the place of Brahmā" (*brahmasthāne*) in order to demonstrate the procedure for the offering of the *arghya*. The word "then" (*tataḥ*) means after the worship of the deities of the [eight] positions, such as Śiva and the others; it does not mean immediately after the previously mentioned rite of the *bali* offerings, because that must be performed only after the fire sacrifice (*homa*).
Because it was established in the previous chapter. "In the place of Brahmā" means in the four-padded space in the center of the mandala.
(3–4) He describes the worship of the Earth, beginning with the word "tataḥ" (then): after the worship of Vāsudeva and the others, in that place of Brahmā.
The meaning is that one should worship the Earth, the sustainer of all worlds. He describes her meditation [as follows]: "of beautiful form" (surūpām), and so forth.
Then, by means of the mantra of her own name, [one worships] the supreme [deity] consisting of all the immortals.
Having meditated, one should worship with devotion that man who consists of the site (vāstu).
Then, the wise one should prepare a foundation with unbroken rice grains in the Brahma-position;
upon that, he should place the consecrated pitcher together with the *vardhanī* vessel.
It should be made of gold, or silver, or even of clay; it must be firm, new,
filled with all kinds of seeds and medicinal herbs, and adorned with gold and silver.
It should be completely filled with precious gems and water purified by a cloth,
provided with excellent sprouts, and anointed with white sandalwood paste.
Having adorned it well with flowers and perfumed it with excellent incense,
it was wrapped in a pair of clean white cloths.

5. "Then" means immediately after the worship of the Earth. "With his own name-mantra" means with the mantra *oṃ vāstupuruṣāya namaḥ*. This is according to the statement from the *Brahmapurāṇa* cited in the *Vāstuyāgatattva*: "The name of every being, preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and ending with the word of salutation (*namaḥ*), is designated as its mantra."

Regarding the phrase "consisting entirely of all the immortals": at the time when the Vāstupuruṣa falls from heaven downward, the deities such as Brahmā, Indra, Īśa, Parjanya, and others, who reside upon his various limbs, fall along with him;
and because scripture declares that their residence upon his limbs is constant and unchanging, he consists entirely of all the immortals. And that—

Then, though the gods, Brahmā, and even the wielder of the trident were terrified, it was seized on all sides by Dānavas, Asuras, and Rākṣasas.
