Because it is the dwelling place of all the gods, it is designated as *Vāstu*; this is to be understood from the statement in the *Matsya Purāṇa* (227).
6. Now, he indicates the placement of the jar dedicated to the deity Brahmā and its location with the words "in the place of Brahmā" (*brahmasthāne*).
This means that after having placed unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) as a support in the central area consisting of four squares, [the jar is placed] upon them.
7–9. He describes the different types of jars to be installed and the sequence of their installation with the verse beginning "golden" (*haimam*), etc.
[This continues] up to the end of the section beginning with "veṣṭitam.
Then, the practitioner of mantra (mantrī), having placed the water-pot (kalaśa) in the station of Brahmā, should worship it.
And in that [place], he beheld the four-faced god, the lord of creatures, whose very form is the mantra.
With perfumes, flowers, incenses, and most enchanting food offerings,
he then stands outside the mandala in the east, facing the east.
The preceptor, having taken the ritual materials, should satisfy the deities beginning with the planets;
then the mantra-practitioner should satisfy those beginning with Brahmā using clarified butter, sesame seeds, and barley.
The wise man should satisfy Prajāpati with a hundred oblations, and he should satisfy the other gods with ten oblations each. || 13 ||
Then the knower of mantras should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ";
thereafter, having prostrated, made his request, and performed the recitation for well-being (svastivācana).
Having properly grasped the water-pitcher, O Lord of Gods, one should cause a stream of water to revolve clockwise around the mandala along the path of the thread.

10. Regarding what was previously indicated in the seventh verse by the phrase "one should establish the jar upon that," he instructs how to perform that very act of establishing the jar according to the prescribed ritual in the words "at the Brahma-place.

12. "Having taken the requisites" means having taken the implements for the fire-offerings (*homa*) and other rites that will be described hereafter. The suffix *-ktvā* (in *gṛhya*) [indicates the sequence of actions].
The substitution of *yava* [for *tila*] is an archaic (Vedic) usage. Regarding the phrase "grahādīn" (the planets, etc.), the reading "brahmādīn" (Brahmā, etc. is maintained in the *Vaidikasarvasva*.

By the term "grahādīn," the oblation to the nine planets (*navagrahahoma*) is indicated. Following that, he describes the oblation to the deities beginning with Brahmā, starting with the word "ghṛtaiḥ" (with clarified butter). However, in the *Vaidikasarvasva*, the oblation is described as being performed with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) consisting of sesame seeds and barley mixed with honey and smeared with clarified butter.
By the phrase "Brahmā and others" (*brahmādīn*), there is the inclusion of Śiva and the other deities situated both inside and outside the mandala.
(13) Now, he states which deity among Brahmā and the others has how many oblations (*homa*): "The Lord of Creatures" (*prajeśam*), etc.
(15). Regarding the term "having taken up" (*pragṛhya*): [it refers to] the *karkarī* and the *vardhanī*, which were previously placed upon the head of the *brahmakumbha*.
As before, one should rotate the seven seed-syllables along that path (or, as in manuscripts *k* and *saṃlikhet*, one should inscribe them).
One should likewise cause the excavation to be made at an auspicious location in a most beautiful manner. (These two lines are in manuscript *ka*).
[Not in the manuscript.
Then, one should dig a pit in the center measuring one cubit in dimension;
one should dig four finger-breadths below that, well-measured.
Then, having smeared it with cow dung, one should adorn it with sandalwood paste;
having placed white flowers and unbroken rice grains (akṣata) in the center. || 18 ||
The preceptor, facing the east, should meditate upon the four-armed deity amidst the sound of musical instruments and auspicious songs, and the excellent chanting of the Vedas.

Having taken [the vessel], one should perform the circumambulation; however, one must not take another water-pot (*karkarī*). In the fourth chapter on the offering of the *arghya* (*saurakāṇḍa*), it is stated: "Having ensured the peace of the world, the Guru should then cause the *arghya* to be offered. Having thus introduced the procedure, the Guru, having properly lifted the jar (*kumbha*) with the chanting of the *brahmaghoṣa* and other sounds, should sprinkle [it] upon the Brahma-sector.

"Then one should rotate the *vardhanī*," and so forth; for by such statements, there is an instruction to rotate the *vardhanī* preceded by the lifting of the *brahmakumbha*. Furthermore, there is no authority for setting aside the *vardhanī* employed in the ritual action to take up another *vardhanī*. According to Hemacandra’s lexicon, "the *vardhanī* is a *galantikā* (a small water-pot)."

Thus says Bhānujidīkṣita in his commentary on the Amarakośa; and the Amarakośa itself states: "Karkarī, ālu, and galantikā [are synonyms]. Therefore, the words *vardhanī* and *karkarī* have identical meanings.
(17) Now, he describes the making of the pit for the offering of the *arghya* water, beginning with the word "tataḥ" (then); [the phrase] "in the middle" refers to...
"In the middle region of the site-ground" means in the place of Brahmā (*brahmasthāna*).

Here, the Smārta Bhaṭṭācāryas have stated that the construction of the pit (*khāta*) is to be made in the space of Ākāśa in the southeast (*āgneyī*); and even now, such is the practice. According to that statement of the Smārtas, [the word] "middle" (*madhya*) found here in the manuscripts *kha* and *ga* [is to be understood as referring to that location].

The reading "on the ground" (bhūmau) is not inconsistent; however, since the reading "in the center" (madhye) is also observed in the Devīpurāṇa as cited in the Vāstuyāgatattva, that very reading has been adopted in the root text.
O best of gods, the knower of mantras should offer the *arghya* with the water from the pitcher;
having taken up the *karkarī*, he should then fill that pit with water.
In that [place], scattering pure, highly fragrant white flowers strewn with all kinds of jewels, one should recite "Om" while remaining mindful.
One should examine that whirlpool by casting an unbroken grain of rice with the beginning of the Veda;
it will be auspicious if it turns to the right, and from that, it will be inauspicious if it turns to the left.
The wise man should fill that pit with seeds of rice, barley, and so forth;
he should then completely fill the pit with pure earth produced from the field.
O best of gods, having thus performed the offering of arghya according to the rite,
one should present gold, a cow, and a pair of garments to the preceptor.
The architect and the astrologer should be honored, and one should worship the Vaiṣṇavas according to one's ability.
Having fed the Brāhmaṇas, one should cause songs, dances, and other such performances to be held. || 26 ||
Then one should carefully excavate it down to the water level;
a foreign object situated below a man's height will not cause harm within the house. || 26 ||
In a palace, a defect-causing splinter may exist as far as the edge of the water;
therefore, the ground for a palace must be cleared as far as the edge of the water. (27)
23 | Regarding "with seeds": with the seven types of seeds, such as rice (*vrīhi*) and others, as previously mentioned in the commentary.

26–27 | Thus, after the offering of the *arghya* water and the feeding of Brahmins, etc., [the author] teaches a specific procedure for the removal of potential thorns—whether the thorns are known or unknown—by means of the previously mentioned signs. Thereupon...
Thus:
[it extends] as far as stone, or gravel, or as far as the earth (or the sky).
Having struck and leveled that [ground], one should then commence the sacrifice (yāga). || 28 ||
Thus ends the tenth chapter, on the offering of the arghya, in the Ādikāṇḍa of the *Hayaśīrṣa Mahāpañcarātra*, the twelve-thousand-verse [treatise]. || 10 ||
The cumulative number of verses from the beginning is 196.

One should carefully excavate that region intended for the site (*vāstu*), which has been purified by the preparatory rites (*parikarma*) for the pacification of the previously mentioned defects of the site. To what extent? He says: "down to the water-level" (*jalāntam*). While the excavation is being performed...

The meaning is: as long as water does not rise from the lower region [of the excavation]. Once the emergence of water has begun, further digging is no longer necessary. And he states that this applies only to the case of a palace (*prāsāda*), and not to ordinary houses (*gṛha*) and the like—namely, "below a man's height. In a house, a stake (*śalya*) situated below ground level measured by the height of a man does not bring about any defect; however, in a palace...

The meaning is that earth, once purified by digging down to water, certifies itself as being free of thorns (*aśalyā*), because a thorn situated beneath it lacks the capacity to produce its effect. Since it is the palace alone that is the subject under discussion here, he concludes with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

28. In that very context, he states another sequence: "up to rock" (*śilāntam*). When digging into the earth and water has not yet emerged, one should continue the excavation until reaching rocks, gravel, black soil, or other such ground beneath the surface. This is because beneath hard rocks and the like, there may be obstacles such as bones or charcoal.

The intended meaning is that because entry is impossible due to the antiquity of the black earth, there is the possibility of the presence of a core (śalya) within it. Regarding the word *ākoṭya*: having struck with a mallet or similar tools that ground which has been purified in this manner, one should commence the sacrifice to be described; such is the meaning.
Chapter Eleven:
(The consecration of the stone slab, therein the consideration of days, and the characteristics of bricks, etc.)
The Blessed One said: Hereafter, I shall explain the consecration known as "the feet" (pāda).
In front, a square pavilion with an altar should be constructed. || 1 ||
It should be auspicious, measuring ten or twelve cubits in length and one-fourth as wide;
it should be adorned with variegated banners, flags, and plantain trees. || 2 ||

1. Now, immediately after the offering of the *arghya*, since the *pātālayāga* (subterranean sacrifice) is to be performed, this chapter on the consecration of the stone (*śilādhivāsana*) is commenced with the words "from here onwards" (*ataḥparam*), for the purpose of defining the nature of the stone-seat (*śilādhvāsana*) which is an ancillary part of that [sacrifice].
In this regard, it should be noted that what is called the *pātālayāga* is the fire-oblation (*homa*) to be described in the forthcoming chapter.

It is a specific ritual activity consisting of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the bricks intended for the commencement of the altar-platform (*vedikā*) and the temple (*prāsāda*) to be built in a subterranean excavation; this follows the performance of the entire cycle of rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*, as prescribed by the injunctions, upon ground purified by the previously mentioned procedures. And that [consecration] is the consecration of the bricks.

Since the pedestal (vedikā) serves as the foundation for the temple by acting as its base—just as a pedestal supports the body of a temple—it follows that the installation of the pedestal is itself the installation of the temple’s foundation. This is expressed by the phrase "the installation known as the feet.
The term "in front" (agrataḥ) means in front of the ground intended to serve as the site for the temple that is about to be constructed.

Regarding the phrase "in front here" (*atra agrataḥ*), even though the specific location of the "front" is not determined, one should set aside ten cubits for the division of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). This is because of the statement from the *Mahākapila-pañcarātra* cited in the *Vaidika-sarvasva*:
"As in the consecration of a deity, so too in the consecration of the present temple, [one should prepare] for the sake of the pavilion..."

It is appropriate to take possession of a space on the terrace of the palace whose upper edge is separated by ten cubits, because no specific measurement has been prescribed and because there is no contradiction.
He states the dimensions of this pavilion: "ten or twelve cubits. Now, in the previous verse, it was [described] as being with a pedestal.
Thus it has been stated. To the question of what the measurement of the altar (*vedikā*) is, he says: "extended by four parts.
(p. 64) One should construct four sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) and four arches (*toraṇa*) in due order.
The placement of the pitchers (kumbha-nyāsa) and the bricks (iṣṭakā-nyāsa), as well as the two door-pillars and the vow (vrata)—indeed, that which rests upon the archway (toraṇa). || 3 ||
One should perform all of this on an auspicious day;
indeed, the worship of the gods and Brahmins must be performed on every such occasion.
One who understands the proper time should perform the worship of Kālajña and the worship of the architects; however, the work of building a dwelling should not be commenced during the rainy season.
At the end of the third part of the dark fortnight, and at the beginning of the second [part] of the bright fortnight,
one should avoid the fourth, the ninth, and also the fourteenth lunar day.
The day of Mars (Tuesday) should be avoided, as well as the karana known as Viṣṭi;
it is afflicted by fear arising from portents originating from the earth, the atmosphere, and the heavens.
A wise person should perform their work when the moon and stars are favorable, and not when the moon is afflicted by planetary influences or struck by the Vyatīpāta yoga.
And in this matter, the following fixed asterisms are praised: Nairṛta, Śakra-devata, Puṣya, Pauṣṇa, Sāvitra, Vāyavya, and likewise Vaiṣṇava.

The altar (vedikā) should be made with a length equal to one-fourth of the pavilion (maṇḍapa). Consequently, the meaning is that the pavilion should be made with a length equal to one-fourth of that altar. Here, there is a reference to the word "altar," even though it is a subordinate element, because it is present in the mind [of the listener].

3–5 | The characteristics of the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) and the arches (*toraṇa*) will be explained in the thirty-fourth chapter. Regarding the term "pitcher" (*kumbha*): by the passage beginning with "the ritual placement of the pitcher" (*kumbhanyāsa*), those various specific details—such as the auspicious and inauspicious times and so forth—are demonstrated for the initial ritual placement of the pitcher (*kumbhanyāsa*) and other rites that are about to be described.
O best of gods, when the fixed portion of the ascendant is stable and the natal ascendant possesses the nature of an *upacaya* house,
and a benefic planet is situated in a quadrant or a trine for that person; (10)
If malefic planets are situated in a house of increase (upacaya), then one may perform the task;
however, one should diligently avoid a malefic planet situated in the *kendra* in all undertakings.
Whatever quadrant is conjoined with a benefic, such a leaf is indeed void; however, that which is conjoined with a benefic in the lord of the fortnight (the Moon) should be known as not at all small.
One should diligently fill the pit, foot by foot, in due order.

A hand-span (one cubit) of earth measuring eight finger-breadths, or [a measure of] bricks and so forth, having been repeatedly sprinkled with water from jars made of gold and other materials... || 13 ||
Then one should perform the hammering with mallets made from the wood of the *brahmavṛkṣa*;
one should fill the excavation until it is three-quarters full and make it perfectly level.

12. In the previous chapter, beginning with the words "Then he should dig that," it was stated that after constructing a pit for the purpose of purifying the ground, one should level it by striking with a mallet. Now, he describes the ritual action to be performed within that pit, starting with the word "he should fill. That pit should be filled in due order, according to the sequence to be described hereafter, [filling it] foot by foot...
One should complete one quarter at a time, but not with the desire to delay; rather, one should finish the entire task of completion all at once.
The meaning is that by acting in such a way, and by avoiding the transgression of the proper sequence, a weakness of the ground (bhūmi) may arise.
(13–14) He states the sequence of completion with the words beginning "eight finger-breadths" (*aṣṭāṅgula*). Here, this should be understood as follows:

First, having filled [the pit] eight *aṅgulas* deep with earth and sprinkled water there, one should strike it with hammers made from the wood of the *brahmavṛkṣa*; then, above that, one should fill it up to the height of a cubit (*hasta*) with bricks and other materials. In this manner:

The filling with earth, bricks, and so forth, as well as the intermittent sprinkling of water and striking with mallets, should be performed until this excavation remains with only a single foot's depth remaining.
It should be understood that the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "with bricks and so forth" is intended to include stone, lime, and other materials appropriate for the specific temple.
Since such an arrangement of distinctions is observed everywhere,
the wise teacher should sprinkle that ground with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). (15)
[It should be] made of gold or copper, filled with water from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), containing grains of gold-rice, and adorned with mango sprouts.
One should sprinkle it with water consecrated by the *abhijapta* mantra using a ritual jar (*kalaśa*).
Thereby, even ground that may be possessed of defects shall become pure.
Having thus purified the ground, the wise man should then worship the site (vāstu);
having stabilized the Brahma-place, he should thereafter take up the bricks.
Now listen to the measurement and the characteristics of the bricks:
they should be well-formed, endowed with the proper marks, and measured at twelve finger-breadths. (19)
They were distinguished by their great extent and detailed classification, prepared with skill;
they were perfectly cooked, of the right proportions, uniform in color, and captivating to the mind.
The bricks should be made stainless, square, and well-proportioned; those with chipped corners are not recommended, as they lack the likeness of hands and feet. || 21 ||
Those [lines] which are mixed with sugar, black in color, and strewn with bone-charcoal—what should the teacher do after that? He says: "The teacher" (verse 17).
What would result from that? He says: "Then" (verse 18).

18. Then, as to what one should do next, he says: "In this manner" (*evam*). Regarding "the place of Brahmā" (*brahmasthānam*): the meaning is that when the pit has been filled to three-quarters, there is a location consisting of four squares—which falls within the previously constructed sixty-four-square mandala—and which constitutes the center of the *vāstu*.

19. Now, as the consecration of the bricks (iṣṭakādhivāsana) is to be performed, he defines the required measurement and characteristics of the bricks, from the words "of the bricks" up to the end of the verse on page 67.
Those which are discolored, have a faint odor, and are thick protuberances; || 22 ||
In a temple made of bricks, the placement of bricks (iṣṭakānyāsa) should be performed using bricks that are not inferior, uneven, broken, shattered, or defective.
On the stone, one should arrange the placement of stones; on the gravel, one should place pebbles. One should take up exactly nine beautiful copper jars. || 24 ||
Having gathered all the necessary materials, one should consecrate the bricks;
having constructed a pavilion in the northeast, one should likewise construct a pavilion in the east for the purpose of the ritual bathing.
Then one should perform the bathing of the water-jars and the bricks with the five astringents (pañcakaṣāya) and with water containing all medicinal herbs.
22. "And those with weak fragrance," and therefore "those that are undercooked" are not desired; "but that which is broken" is [also rejected]—this is the reading preserved in the *Vaidikasarvasva*.
23–24. He describes the different types of bricks and so forth used as materials for the various kinds of palaces (*prāsāda*) with the words: "It should be made."

Now, since the consecration of the bricks (*iṣṭakādhivāsana*) and the sacrifice of the underworld (*pātālayāga*) are to be described, he states the procurement of the materials for their constituent parts with the words beginning "nine indeed" (verses 25–26). He describes the bathing that is a constituent part of that consecration with the words "in the northeast" (*aiśānyām*); here, one should [construct] a pavilion in the northeast.
Having constructed a pavilion there to the east of the nine previously mentioned pitchers, one should perform the ritual bathing of the nine bricks; such is the sequence of the connection.
By the phrase "one should likewise bathe the bricks," it is indicated that after the instruction for the bathing of the bricks, one should then bathe those pitchers.

By the word "Budhaḥ" (the wise one), the ritual bathing with water-pots (*kalaśasnāna*) will also be described. However, according to the readings of the manuscripts *kh* and *g*, it appears that there are not two pavilions (*maṇḍapa*), but rather that the bathing of the water-pots and the bricks should be performed in a single pavilion, namely the Īśāna-maṇḍapa. But the authors of the *Vaidikasarvasva* [state otherwise].
And likewise with scented water from jars well-filled with water,
joined with gold and rice, and anointed with fragrant sandalwood. || 27 ||

With the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and also with "śanno devī," as well as with "taratsamandī" and the Pāvamānī hymns; [the two quarters beginning with "tarat" are not found in manuscript k]. || 28 ||
"uduttamaṃ varuṇa," "imam me," likewise "varuṇasya," and also "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat. (29)
Likewise, one should bathe the bricks with water-pots while reciting the Śrīsūkta;
the wise man should bathe those pots while reciting the Śrāyantīya hymn.
Then one should apply fragrant sandalwood paste as anointment;
thereafter, one should provide clothing with garments, and then with flowers.
On an excellent bedstead, having installed [the image] in a pavilion, one should worship it with various kinds of food and rice, as well as with fragrances and beautiful flowers. (32)
One should diligently offer incense, lamps, and food offerings to them;
having done this, one should then properly perform the fire-sacrifice (homa) with bricks.
In that pavilion, however, one should indeed draw an auspicious Vaiṣṇava mandala.
Regarding the phrase "of the jars" (*kumbhānām*) here, some read it as "of the excellent ones" (*utkṛṣṭānām*), interpreting its meaning accordingly;
thus, everything has been cast into doubt. He describes the bathing of the bricks with the words beginning with "atha," etc.
[He] should bathe the brick, up to the end [of the verse].
(30) He describes the bathing with nine jars by means of the [verse] beginning with "śrāyantīyam.
(31) He describes what is to be done immediately after the bathing by means of the passage beginning with "tataḥ" (then).
33. Now, after the worship of the bricks, he describes the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the words beginning "In this manner" (*evam*):
"(One) should worship Viṣṇu there, and then one should offer oblations into the fire in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). (34)
Having first generated the Vaiṣṇava fire according to the rules with a concentrated mind,
he should perform the offering of fuel sticks with the twelve-syllable vidyā. || 35 ||
One should perform the two libations (āghāra) and the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) with the syllable Om alone;
thereafter, one should offer eight oblations in sequence using the eight-syllable mantra, each syllable taken separately.
Having offered clarified butter with the *vyāhṛtis*—namely "Bhūr," "Bhuvaḥ," and "Svaḥ"—in due order to the Lords of the World, and indeed to Agni, Soma, and the Planets; 37.
Having offered oblations with the mantra "To Puruṣottama," one should then offer the *vyāhṛtis*.
Then, having performed the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta*), one should subsequently offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). || 38 ||
O sinless one, the image-keepers should properly offer oblations of sesame seeds mixed with ghee into the sacrificial pits, using either the twelve-syllable mantra or the Vedic mantras.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, on the consecration of the stone, in the Ādikāṇḍa of the *Hayaśīrṣa Mahāpañcarātra*, the twelve-thousand-verse [treatise]. 11.
The total number of verses from the beginning is 258 (34).

Regarding the phrase "vaiṣṇavam," the reading "bhadrākhyam" (known as Bhadra) is maintained by all Vedic authorities for the *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala. Having worshipped Viṣṇu in that maṇḍala, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
One should perform [the rite]. The characteristics of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) will be described [in the following]. (35) The Vaiṣṇava fire will be defined in the thirty-sixth chapter.
(39) Regarding the statement that "one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*"), he states the specific detail therein as "twelve," etc.
The meaning is that one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation) either with the twelve-syllable mantra or with the four mantras beginning with the Vedas.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter.
(The Pātālayāga: the distinction of deities, the distinction of the arrangement of the sacred seats, and the praise of the construction of the temple.
The Blessed Lord said:
Then the preceptor, adorned with all ornaments, facing the east, should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the pitchers and likewise the ritual placement of the bricks.
Having smeared the ground with cow dung, one should place nine jars according to the rule:
eight in the cardinal directions and one likewise in the center.
Having prepared them joined with the five jewels and combined with auspicious medicinal herbs—

The meaning is that one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of those [deities] who have been consecrated by the procedures of the preceding chapter.

He states that sequence with the words beginning "having smeared" (*vilipya*), etc.; the meaning is that there are nine pitchers—eight in the order starting from the northeast (*īśāna*) toward the south, and one in the center.
4–5 | He describes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the deities within those jars with the words "the lotus" and so forth.
Having thus arranged them—here, [one places] the conch shell—one should not move these jars again. || 5 ||
Having placed eight bricks upon the pitcher in due order,
one should first place a brick in the northeastern corner.

the deities of the bricks are the powers (śaktis), beginning with Vimalā.
She, who is to be placed for the sake of grace, should be installed according to the rule in the center;

"O brick, grant what is desired; I am performing the installation.

Then, being composed, one should perform the *garbhādhāna* (conception rite) in the central space. [Note:

The reading "pustakadhṛtaḥ" (held by the manuscript) has not been included in the root text, as it would result in redundancy due to the mention of "and the conch" (*śaṅkhaṃ ca*) in the fourth quarter of the verse. Regarding the phrase "in due order," the placement of the bricks is to be done exactly in the sequence starting from the northeast (*īśāna*), just as with the water-pots (*kalaśa*).

The meaning is that it should be performed. However, the authors of the *Vaidika-sarvasva* state that after the laying of the bricks (*iṣṭakā-nyāsa*)—with the formula "Then indeed the circumambulation [is performed] for the God"—the installation of the water-jars (*kalaśa-sthāpana*) should also follow in this same sequence according to the order of the principal elements (*pradhāna-krama*). What is this?
No measurement is seen [for this].

(6–8) Regarding "of the jar": by that same sequence, the laying of the bricks (*iṣṭakā*) should also be performed. Since it is stated here "proceeding clockwise" (*pradakṣiṇam*), the entire ritual procedure—from the water-jar (*kalaśa*) up to the laying of the bricks—should be done starting from the northeast (*īśāna*).
It should be understood that the movement must be performed in a clockwise direction (*prādakṣiṇyena*), since no specific [direction] is mentioned. Regarding the term "powers" (*śaktayaḥ*):

the authors of the *Vaidikasarvasva* maintain that by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "Vimalā and so forth," there is an inclusion of the eight [powers], namely: Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Hriyā, Saṃyogā, Prahvī, Satyā, Īśānā, and Anugrahā. Thus, they range from Vimalā to Īśānā.
The eight [deities] in the directions, and Anugrahā in the center—these are the nine deities of the bricks (iṣṭakā).
9. Regarding the invocation during the laying of the bricks, he says: "Avyaṅga" (verse 10).
He describes the *garbhādhāna* (conception/impregnation) rite with the words: "garbha" (verse 11). This is what is called *garbhādhāna*.
"O Lord of Gods, [the vessel] twelve finger-breadths in width, upon which the lotus is the presiding deity," and so forth (p. 72). || 10 ||
O Lord, the preceptor should take earth from ten locations:
from the ocean, a mountain, a river, a lake, a sacred ford, and likewise from a threshing floor. (11)
In the dwelling of a crab, in an anthill, at the tip of a bull's horn,
and at the tip of an elephant's tusk— in these places, respectively— 12.
O best of gods, one should take the excellent roots of the red lotus, the [ordinary] lotus, as well as the blue lotus, and the white water-lily.
Realgar, lead, yellow orpiment, antimony, saurāṣṭrī, gorocana, fragrance, mercury, and likewise red ochre; || 14 ||
Vajra, pearl, lapis lazuli, and conch shell;
crystal, topaz, and likewise moonstone. || 15 ||
A wise person should diligently acquire a great sapphire and a ruby.
The best of preceptors should accept śāli rice, nīvāra, niṣpāva, barley, mung beans, horse gram, sesame, wheat, and kulmāṣa. || 17 ||
Gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, and lead; likewise the tortoise, the serpent, the lotus, the conch, the discus, and the bow. (18)
O highly fortunate one, he should make everything, including the mace, out of gold;
having brought all of this together, he should indeed place it within the womb-vessel.
The placement, according to the prescribed rite, of the specific vessel to be described— which is filled with ocean-clay and other materials—
within the foundation of the altar (*vedikā*) of the temple that is about to be constructed; this very point he explains with the words beginning "in the middle," and so forth.
Twelve finger-breadths in width and four finger-breadths in height,
smooth, uncracked, lotus-shaped, and very beautiful. (20)
Silver from the moon, as well as copper from the earth, is praised for use as a vessel for the embryo;
for the pitcher formerly placed in the station of Brahmā was consecrated to the deity Śrī.
Above that, having placed a cloth over the eyes, one should perform the sprinkling with cow's urine;
above that, one should place *darbha* grass upon the Brahmins.
The vessel. || 22 ||
For Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, however, without a cloth,
one should clean the vessel with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) after making it stainless.
Then, having grasped it with both hands, one should contemplate within that very [space] the entire circle of the earth, together with its oceans and its mountains. 24.
20–21 | He states the womb-vessel (*garbhabhājana*): "twelve," etc. The lunar vessel is made of gold;

for it is stated in the *Amara-kośa*: "In the word *svarṇa*, there are two meanings: 'abundant' and 'moon'. The copper vessel is made of bronze; for the *Medinī-kośa* states: "*Śulva* means copper, [used] in sacrificial rites, as a support, or in proximity to water."
21–22. Now, as to where that vessel containing the embryo should be placed and in what manner, he says: "in the Brahma-position.

Regarding the word "placed," it means one should place [the vessels] in the eight directions according to rule, and likewise one in the center; this is in accordance with [verse 12.2]: "In the center, in the Brahma-position, [one should place] the kalaśa, and likewise the Padma, Mahāpadma, Makara, and Kacchapa."

"Likewise Mukunda, Nanda, Nīla, Śaṅkha, and Padminī" (12.4). Here, by the word *padminī*, the placement (*nyāsa*) of that which is understood to have the goddess Śrī as its deity is indicated; the meaning is that one should place the *garbhabhājana* above that placed pitcher. And this [is for] the Brāhmaṇas. For Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras...
He states the distinction with the words "of the Kṣatriyas" (verse 23).
When the vessel for the embryo has been thus arranged, he describes the ritual actions with the words beginning "pure" (vimalam), etc.
Having thus meditated upon the earth as being joined with the lords of the directions and continents, and situated above Ananta, one should conceive of it as the vessel.
Having taken clay produced from the ocean, one should construct a circular enclosure proceeding clockwise.
A mountain-born image should be placed in the east, and likewise, a river-born image in the south.
One born from a lake should be placed in the western part, and likewise one born from a sacred ford (tīrtha) in the north;
one born from a threshing floor should be made in the southeast, while one born from a crab (kulīra) should be in the southwest.

The one born from an anthill should be placed in the northwest, that born from a bull's horn in the northeast, and that produced from an elephant tusk in the center; these should be installed in due order.
To the east of the red lotus, however, is the root of the lotus;
to the south is that of the blue lotus, and to the north is that of the white water-lily.

One should place the minerals, such as realgar and the rest, in the sequence starting from the east, and likewise the varieties of jewels, such as the vajra and so forth, according to that same sequential order. (30)
And one should sow seeds such as rice and others in that very place.
Gold should be placed in the east, and likewise silver in the south. (31)
In the western part there is iron, and likewise tin in the north;
in the southeast is the form of a tortoise, and likewise Ananta in the southwest.
Then, one should place a lotus in the northwest (vāyavyā), a conch in the northeast (īśāna), and a bow, a discus, and a mace in the position of Brahmā (brahmasthāna).
Having thus performed the union (*samāyoga*) and sprinkled it with the twelvefold mantra of knowledge,
one should then place it to the south and commence the rite of fire-offering (*homakarman*). || 34 ||
Having offered twelve oblations of clarified butter with the twelve-syllable vidyā, likewise to the eight world-protectors and to Nārāyaṇa as well. (35)
From all seeds [or cooling things, k], from all elements (dhātu), and indeed from all worlds;
likewise from rivers, oceans, sacred fords (tīrtha), and mountains. || 36 ||
From the lakes and from the hosts, and likewise from the netherworlds;
from the bulls, the elephants of the quarters, and from the best of gods, O most excellent of gods.
One should also offer oblations with the *vyāhṛtis*, joined with the utterance of *svāhā* at the end;
and one should perform the introductory oblation according to the very rule for the residual drops (*saṃpāta*).
One should complete the pouring of the clarified butter into the middle of the vessel containing the embryo;
then, having covered the vessel, one should grasp it with the hand while it is heated. (39)
One should recite the eight-syllable mantra as well as the twelve-syllable mantra;
having recited them, facing the east, one should meditate upon the Earth with the mind.

34–39 | Now he states the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homavidhi*). Regarding the phrase "then to the south" (*atha dakṣiṇataḥ*): the meaning is that the vessel containing the embryo (*garbhabhājana*) should be placed on the south, that is, in the southern part. Therefore, according to the authors of the *Vaidikasarvasva*, the oblation is performed in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) itself by the preceptor (*ācārya*).
Having meditated upon the entire ground, one should utter this mantra in a solitary place on a site adorned with a mountain-throne. (41)
O Goddess, you who are clothed by the ocean, conceive a child;
O Nandā, daughter of Vasiṣṭha, bring joy through your offspring along with the Vasus.
O victor, descendant of Bhṛgu, who brings victory to all creatures!
O perfect one, descendant of Aṅgiras, fulfill my every desire. (43)
O noble lady, daughter of Kāśyapa, bestow upon me an auspicious thought, for this place is endowed with every seed and covered with all kinds of jewels and medicinal herbs. (44)
Be victorious, O beautiful Nandā, daughter of Vasiṣṭha! O Goddess, daughter of Prajāpati, O square one, O most exalted one, may you take delight here.
O fortunate one, O auspicious one, O blessed one, daughter of Kaśyapa, may you dwell happily in this house,
which is honored by supreme teachers and adorned with perfumes and garlands.
O Goddess Bhūti, who brings prosperity, may you dwell happily in the house of the descendant of Bhṛgu;
O daughter of the sage Aṅgiras, you who are unmanifest, imperishable, and perfect.

"O brick, grant what is desired; I am performing the consecration. [The mantra consisting of the four quarters beginning with "avyakta" and ending with "kārayāmyaham" is not present in the manuscripts *kh* and *g*.
...in the possession of the lord of the land, the lord of the city, and the lord of the house. (48)
"Be the increaser of human wealth, elephants, horses, and cattle.
Having spoken thus, he then sprinkled the pit with cow's urine. (49)

41. He states the prayer-mantras for the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*): *oṃ ekānte* and so forth. (p. 77) Having performed [the ritual], one should cause the womb (*garbha*) to be fixed [or: caused to be placed]. (k reads *garttaṃ*; kh reads *garbhaṃ*)
Endowed with all that is auspicious, the rite of impregnation (garbhādhāna) should take place at night; gold shall be the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 50 ||
Likewise, a milch cow and a pair of garments should be given, and similarly, a milch cow should be given to the image-keepers (mūrtipās). || 51 ||
Having thus deposited the womb (garbha), one should thereafter place a ninth brick;
then, having covered the womb with the mechanical device (yantra), one should fill it with bricks.
Thereafter, one should construct the pedestal (pīṭha) according to the proportions of the great temple;
the best pedestal should be half the height of the temple.

A wise person should construct the pedestal for Vāsudeva as the best; the middle one should be one-quarter less than that, and the smallest should be one-quarter less than the middle, according to the vertical measurement.
One may construct a pedestal for others according to one's own desire; listen specifically to the description of the supreme pedestal for the Four-faced Lord (Brahmā) and the Sun. || 55 ||

49–51 | Having thus made the prayer, one should again place the vessel containing the embryo into that pit which has been sprinkled with cow’s urine. He states the time for the *garbhādhāna* (conception rite) and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) with the words beginning "The *garbhādhāna*...
(verse 52). Then, he describes the filling of that pit with the words beginning "Thus... (verse 53).
53–55 | Thus, having filled the excavation according to the sequence previously described, one should perform the construction of the pedestal (*pīṭhabandha*) therein.
The pedestal construction is the temple altar (*vedikā*), from which the walls of the house begin. That pedestal construction is of three kinds:
superior, middling, and inferior. He states that very threefold division with the words beginning "the superior pedestal" (*pīṭhottama*).
He describes the division of the *pīṭhas* according to the division of deities, beginning with the words "the best" (*uttamam*).
After the binding of the *pīṭha*, one should again perform the *vāstuyajña*.
He who performs this entire installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) based upon the pedestal... [text fragment].
Freed from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
and that mortal who has laid the first brick shall not go to death.
He who, even if he only thinks in his mind, "I shall build a temple for the gods," undoubtedly obtains the fruit of a completed sacrifice. (58)
The evil committed by him against the body perishes on that very day; how much more so, then, when he has constructed a temple according to the prescribed rite? 59.
Whoever should construct a Vaiṣṇava temple endowed with eight bricks,
the fullness of the fruit thereof could not be described by anyone.
Indeed, the extent of the fruit may be inferred from the width of the temple;
one should construct the eastern gate in the middle of the village and facing toward the east.
And in all the intermediate directions, one should likewise face westward;
in the south and the north, as well as in the west, one should face eastward.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, the section on the Pātāla Sacrifice, in the Ādikāṇḍa of the *Hayaśīrṣa Mahāpañcarātra*, the twelve-thousand-verse [treatise]. || 12 ||
The total number of verses from the beginning is 279.
Verses 56–61 state the fruit resulting from the consecration of a temple, beginning with the words "He who this...
Verse 62 states the specific distinction regarding the construction of the doors of temples according to their different locations, beginning with the words "In the middle of a village..."
Chapter Thirteen:
The General Characteristics of Temples, the Variations in Sequence, and the Temple Ending with Seven Stories; therein—
Regarding the specific details, the Blessed Lord said:
"I shall fully describe the temple that is common to all; listen."
One should divide the square field again into sixteen parts. || 1 ||
In its center, one should construct a structure made of iron with four [sides];
one should then determine twelve divisions for the walls and corners.
The height of the shank should be made one-fourth of its length;
the wise [architect] should fashion the height of the *mañjarī* as twice that of the two shanks.
A proper circumambulation should be made with a fourth part of the cluster;
the *nigama* should be made of that same measurement, equal on both sides.
The width at the front should be equal to the pinnacle;
it may also be made double that size, according to what is appropriate for its beauty. || 5 ||

1 | Having described everything up to the construction of the temple (*prāsāda*) and its pedestal (*vedikā*) in the preceding chapter, he begins in this chapter to state the general characteristics of the temple with the words "the temple" (*prāsādam*), etc.
5 | He states the length of the ground situated in front of the temple: "equal to the pinnacle" (*śikhareṇa samam*). [This refers to] the pinnacle of the temple.
In front of the pavilion, one should make the central chamber (garbha) wider by two threads,
and its length should be one-quarter greater than that, at the center.
Adorned with pillars. || 6 ||

Or one should construct the front pavilion (mukhamaṇḍapa) according to the measurement of the interior of the temple; having worshipped the site (vāstu) with eighty-one squares, one should begin the construction of the pavilion.
In the arrangement of the Śukāḍhya door, one should worship the deities situated at the ends of the quarters;
likewise, in the arrangement of the enclosure wall, one should worship those located at the end of the thirty-two [divisions].
This is the general characteristic of a temple;
now hear of another type of temple according to the measurement of the image.
The auspicious pedestal (piṇḍikā) should be made according to the measurement of the image;
the inner sanctum (garbha) should be half the size of the pedestal, and the walls should be equal in measure to the sanctum.
The meaning is that the width should be equal to the height of the ground area situated in front. Regarding the phrase "by double":
where an excess of width enhances the particular beauty of the site, there the width should be made even double; this is the meaning.

6 | 7 | Now, he describes the nature of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) situated in front of the temple with the words beginning "the width," and so forth. He states another alternative method with the words "prāsāda" and so forth. Having set aside the outer twelfth part of the field—which has been divided into sixteen parts according to the measurement of the interior of the temple (*prāsādagarbha*)—as stated in the passage beginning "in the middle of that," etc.

The meaning is that one should construct the front pavilion (*mukhamaṇḍapa*) with the same measurement as the interior portion of the wall consisting of the four central sections. As for the measurement of the eighty-one-square *vāstu* mandala,
it will be explained in some way during the commentary on the ninth chapter, which sets forth the sixty-four-square *vāstu* mandala.
This has been demonstrated. However, the specific details should be sought in the *Viśvakarmaprakāśa* and other such works.
(9) He describes another type of temple (*prāsāda*) with the words "by measurement" (*mānena*).
One should determine the height according to the measurement of the wall's length;
the preceptor (or wise one) should fashion the spire to be twice the height of the wall.
One should fashion the circumambulatory path (bhramaṇa) to be one-fourth the size of the spire.
In front of the pinnacle, there is a portico (mukhamaṇḍapa) measuring one-fourth [of its size]. || 12 ||

The projection of the chariot-arches (rathaka) from the center of the womb-wall should be one-eighth of its width; there, one should fashion the chariot-arches using a third part of the thickness of the enclosing wall (paridhi).
Or one should effect the exit of the chariots by means of that third [line];
three *rāmas* should always be established for each of the three chariots.
For the sake of the pinnacle, one should drop the threads and the jewels;
from above the *śukanāsa*, one should drop the horizontal thread. (This reading is found in manuscripts *kha* and *ga*;
it is not present in manuscript *ka*. || 15 ||
One should have a lion fashioned there, situated at the midpoint of the pinnacle;
having stabilized the *śukanāsā* (the "parrot-nose" projection), one should fix it at the central joint.
And others should likewise place a thread on the sides;

above that, O Lord, let there be its neck, which possesses a dark luster, as desired by the mind. [Note: In the manuscripts *kh* and *g*, the reading "kaśco manasāvarān" is an error; it should be "kaṇṭhe śyāmalasāravān"].
This is the reading recorded in the *Śabdakalpadruma*. || 17 ||
One should not make it with broken shoulders, nor likewise with distorted shoulders;
one should fashion the kalaśa above the height of the vedikā. || 18 ||
The width should be made twice the size of the door, and it must be very beautiful.
[This half-verse is missing in manuscript k.
Having given gold, the wise man should place a branch of the *udumbara* tree, half of which is made of gold.
And having caused the Brahmins to pronounce auspicious blessings with the sound of musical instruments and festive music. || 20 ||
At one-fourth the width of the door, Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa are to be made;
both should be depicted with staffs in their hands and resembling Viśvaksena.
Having placed half a branch, one should place jewels upon it, with an udumbara fruit at the top;
in its center resides the Goddess, the sovereign of the gods, Lakṣmī herself.
That [image], being bathed with a water-pot by the elephants of the quarters, should be so treated; furthermore,
two udumbara branches, adorned with leafy creepers and the like, should be fashioned.
[In this regard, the reading "pittryavantyādibhūṣitau" is seen in manuscript K, but it is not authoritative. || 23 ||
A door is desired to have one branch, three branches, or six branches;
one may also make it nine-branched, but beyond this one should not construct it. (24)
One should diligently adorn the branch with the forms and attributes of the incarnations of Viṣṇu and others.
The height of the enclosure wall should be one-fourth the size of the temple.
The height of the gate-tower (gopura) should be one-quarter less than that of the enclosure wall. [The two lines beginning with "ekabhūmi" are not present in manuscript *k*.]
The pedestal for a deity five cubits in height shall be one cubit in height. || 26 ||
Twice that size, however, is said to be the Garuḍa-maṇḍapa;
it should be constructed starting from one cubit up to thirty cubits.
One should construct [a temple] starting from one floor up to seven floors;
however, for Viṣṇu, there should be a single-floor structure in the northwest, known by the name Nāga.
The temple of Agni should have two stories, while that of Mahendra has three;
the temple of Varuṇa has four parts, and that of Saura should have five stories.
The Saumya temple is to be known as having six stories,
while the Vaiṣṇava has seven. One should likewise construct the Garutvanta temple above, extending in the four directions.
The guru is four times the end. || 30 ||
One should indeed fashion the measurements for the images in the eight directions and above:
Mahāvarāha in the eastern direction and Narasiṃha in the south. (31)
One should worship the god Śrīdhara in the west, Hayaśīrṣaka in the north,
Jāmadagnya in the southeast, and Rāma in the southwest.
One should place Vāmana in the northwest, and Vāsudeva in another location;
on the first floor there should be a bed, and on the second, a seat (or food).
In the third, it is indeed the *sthāna* (posture); in the fourth, the *yāna* (vehicle);
in the fifth, *yoganidrā* (yogic sleep); and in the sixth, there is *yogāsana* (yogic posture). || 34 ||
One should carefully construct the seventh [section], provided with the yoga of its proper location, adorned with various latticed windows, leaf-patterns, creepers, and so forth. (35)
One should arrange various kinds of flowers and other offerings according to their beauty,
following the sequence for the smallest, medium, and largest temples.
The wise, such as the learned Vasubhārgava— [here, although a different reading is held in manuscript K,
it is not clearly understood due to the indistinctness of the letters]—
should provide this composition at the eighth, ninth, and likewise the tenth yoga of the door. (37)
There should never be a piercing of the forehead; listen now, O sinless one, as to how far the temple intended by the builders should extend in cubits. (38)

The flagstaff (dhvaja) should be made with that many finger-breadths or by one-eighth part of the length; it is known as having a single pillar, while the pedestal (vedikā) is considered to have two pillars.
Within the space of the ten bhūmis, one should always fashion four pillars;
O sinless one, the procedure for the archway has thus been described to you. (40)
When a pillar-supported altar is to be constructed at the top of a palace,
then a pillar-supported altar must likewise be constructed by the Vaiṣṇavas.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, on the characteristics of temples, in the Ādikāṇḍa of the *Hayaśīrṣa Mahāpañcarātra*, the twelve-thousand-verse [treatise]. || 13 ||
The total number of verses from the beginning is 310.
O sinless one, listen further to what should be established according to the proper method. || 3 ||

1 | Having described the general characteristics of the temple (*prāsāda*) in the preceding chapter, this chapter is commenced with the words "from here onwards" (*ataḥparam*) and so forth, for the purpose of describing its specific characteristics. Although the characteristics of the temple itself are not explicitly stated here,
in reality (*vastugatyā*), they are [implied] through the description of the sequence for the arrangement of the secondary and primary deities to be installed therein.
Since the specific characteristics of the temple have naturally followed, I shall explain the characteristics of temples;
this is appropriately connected. "Of temples" means the characteristic of their varieties.
2 | 3 | A temple is of three kinds: having five sanctuaries (pañcāyatana), nine sanctuaries (navāyatana), and twelve sanctuaries (dvādaśāyatana). Among these—
That temple which has four shrines at the four corners of its main sanctum is a *pañcāyatana* temple.

Regarding the sequence for installing the deities therein, he says "in the *pañcāyatana*": in the central main shrine of the *pañcāyatana* temple, one installs Vāsudeva; in the southeast shrine, Vāmana; and in the southwest shrine, Narasiṃha.

"One method for the installation of the five deities (*pañcāyatana*) is that one should place Hayaśīrṣa in the Vāyavya shrine and Nṛśūkara in the Īśāna shrine. He states another method: "Listen to another [method].
Having established Nārāyaṇa in the center, one should install Ambikā in the southeast;
having established Bhāskara in the southwest, one should place the Lotus-born (Brahmā) in the northwest.
One should install a liṅga or an image of Rudra in the northeast;
however, one should have Vāsudeva reside in the center of the nine-shrine temple.
Furthermore, one should install Rāma and the others starting from the east and ending with the northeast;
or else, one should install the world-protectors, Indra and the rest, in the eight directions in their proper order.

4 | 5 | "In the center" means: alternatively, one may install Nārāyaṇa in the central sanctuary, Ambikā in the southeast sanctuary, Bhāskara in the southwest sanctuary, Brahmā in the northwest sanctuary, and Rudra or a Liṅga in the northeast sanctuary;
this is another sequence for the five sanctuaries (pañcāyatana). And thus, whichever deity is the primary one according to one's own preference—
It appears that he [the principal deity] should be placed in the central main temple, while the others are to be installed in the other four; thus [ends verses] 5 and 6.

Now, regarding the installation of the nine abodes (*navāyatana*), he describes the sequence for installing the deities with the words "in the nine abodes" (*navāyatane*). In the installation of the nine abodes as well, just as in the case of the five abodes (*pañcāyatana*), the principal abode is in the center.

Having conceptualized eight abodes starting from the east, one should place Rāma and the others in due order within the principal central abode and likewise in the other eight abodes starting from the east. As for Rāma and the others, they are Balarāma, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Narasiṃha, and Varāha. By the term "Rāma and the others," these [are meant].
The specific details of their placement should be observed in the twenty-fourth chapter, the section on the characteristics of the images for the ninefold arrangement (*navavyūha*).
And thus it is said: Vāsudeva is in the central principal sanctuary; Balarāma in the eastern quarter; Pradyumna in the southeast;
Aniruddha in the south; Nārāyaṇa in the southwest; Brahmā in the west; Viṣṇu in the northwest; [and Keśava] in the north.

The meaning is that one should install Narasiṃha in the northeast and Varāha [in the southeast]. Regarding the installation of the deities of the directions, he states another method: "Indra and the others. Thus, having installed Vāsudeva in the center according to the previously mentioned sequence, one should install the world-protectors, Indra and the rest, in order from the east to the northeast.
Alternatively, the ninefold abode (*navāyatana*) is described in another way:
within the arrangement of the five abodes, those who are middling among the six [classes of beings] reside there.
The form of Puruṣottama should be installed in the center by the wise;
Lakṣmī and Vaiśravaṇa should be placed in the east and in the Vaḍabhyā [northwest] respectively.
In the south, the wise one should place the group of Mothers within the mare;
likewise, he should install Īśāna, Skanda, and Gaṇeśa here.
In the western mare, one should place the planets beginning with the Sun;
in the northern mare, one should place the ten [signs] beginning with Pisces.
Caṇḍikā should be installed in the southeast, Ambikā should be placed in the southwest,
Sarasvatī in the northwest, and Padmā in the region of the northeast.
And in the center, one should install the Goddess, as well as Vāsudeva as described,
or Nārāyaṇa, or Śrīdhara, or Vāmana, the destroyer of delusion.
That middle [mandala] consists of twelve bases (āyatanas), while the thirteenth is the center;
O best of gods, hear now the divisions of the deities within this. 13.
One should place Viśvarūpa in the center, and then Keśava and the others in clockwise order, installing them correctly according to the sequence starting from the east.
One should place the middle [line] in that location where one intends to install the image;
this piercing (vedha) is known as the general method, according to the difference in one's desire. || 15 ||
